Comment: This class is specific for the dinucletoide-type electron carriers, such as |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP|. For a class that represent two nucleotides that participate in nucleic acids, please see |FRAME: Dinucleotide-Nucleic-Acid|.

Compound.name: a sugar phosphate
Comment: This compound class stands for generic and unspecified sugar phosphates.

Compound.name: a pterin
Comment: |FRAME: Pterins Pterins| are heterocyclic compounds composed of fused |FRAME: CPD-26401| and |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING| rings (a |FRAME: CPD-15307| ring system), with an amino group in the 2-position and an oxo group in the 4-position of the pyrimidine ring.

Compound.name: a flavonoid
Comment: Flavonoids are a class of plant secondary metabolites. Their name is derived from the Latin word flavus meaning yellow, their colour in nature. In higher plants, flavonoids are involved in UV filtration, symbiotic nitrogen fixation and floral pigmentation. They are the most important plant pigments for flower coloration producing yellow or red/blue pigmentation. The term flavonoids is very generic, and is used to describe any organic molecular entity whose stucture is based on derivatives of a phenyl-substituted |FRAME: CPD-20037 1-phenylpropane| possessing a C15 or C16 skeleton, or such a structure condensed with a C6-C3 lignan precursors. The following are three of the main classes of flavonoids, although many more exist: |FRAME: Flavones Flavones|, which are based on the backbone of |FRAME: CPD-8485| (2-phenylchromen-4-one) |FRAME: Isoflavonoids Isoflavonoids|, which are based on the backbone of |FRAME: CPD-15821| |FRAME: Neoflavonoids Neoflavonoids|, derived from |FRAME: CPD-15822|.

Compound.name: a ketone
Comment: A ketone is a compound with the structure RC(=O)R', where R and R' can be a variety of atoms and groups of atoms. It features a carbonyl group (C=O) bonded to two other carbon atoms. Ketones differ from |FRAME: Aldehydes aldehydes| in that the carbonyl is placed between two carbons rather than at the end of a carbon skeleton.

Compound.name: an A vitamin
Comment: Vitamin A is a group of related compounds that include |FRAME: Retinols retinol|, |FRAME: Retinals retinal|, |FRAME: Retinoates retinoate|, and several provitamin A carotenoids, among which |FRAME: CPD1F-129| is the most important. Vitamin A has multiple functions: it is important for growth and development, for the maintenance of the immune system and for vision. Vitamin A is needed by the retina of the eye in the form of retinal, which combines with protein |FRAME: Opsins opsin| to form the light-absorbing molecule rhodopsin (see |FRAME: PWY-6861|). Vitamin A, in the form of retinoic acid, is also an important hormone-like growth factor for epithelial and other cells. In foods of animal origin, the major form of vitamin A are |FRAME: Retinyl-Esters esters|, primarily |FRAME: CHOCOLA_A|, which are converted to retinol in the small intestine.

Compound.name: factor 430
Synonyms: nickel (I) porphinoid // factor F430 // cofactor F430 // coenzyme F430
Comment: CPD-19766 (often referred to as coenzyme F430) is a nickel containing tetrapyrrole cofactor that is present in all methanogenic bacteria. It was initially observed in 1977 by Jean LeGall in extracts of |FRAME: TAX-145262|. The name factor 430 (F430) was coined by Gunsalus and Wolfe who reported the absorbance maximumat 430 nm Gunsalus78. The compound belongs to the corphins, a class of compounds that combine structural elements of both |FRAME: Corrins corrins| and |FRAME: Porphyrins porphyrins| Eschenmoser86. In 1982 Ellefson et al showed that CPD-19766 is a cofactor of the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.8.4.1| (methyl-coenzyme M reductase) 6954513. This enzyme catalyzes the final step of methane production in all methanogenic bacteria: the reduction of the methyl group in |FRAME: Me-CoM| to CH4. F430 exists in two distinct intracellular pools: either bound to EC 2.8.4.1 or free of protein in the cytosol. Early literature on F430 was confusing due to reports of heterogeneity in F430 samples that depended on the isolation and purification procedures used in different laboratories. Later work showed that F430 exists primarily in two isomeric forms. These forms differ in the relative stereochemical disposition of acid side chains at positions 12 and 13 3356701. The biosynthetic route leading to |FRAME: PWY-5196| was discovered only in 2016 27846569.

Compound.name: a carotene
Comment: Carotenes are a type of carotenoids, isoprenoid pigments occurring naturally in plants and some microorganisms, that are purely hydrocarbons (with no oxygen).

Comment: In this group of digalactosyldiacylglycerols, the length of the two acyl chains, and the location and number of the double bonds varies. For each of the group members, the total number of carbon atoms in the two acyl chains adds up to 34, and the total number of double bonds in the two acyl groups adds up to 1.

Compound.name: an aliphatic diamine

Compound.name: a steroid acid

Compound.name: a 7-deazapurine
Comment: Pyrrolopyrimidine nucleosides analogs, collectively referred to as deazapurines, are an important class of structurally diverse compounds found in a wide variety of biological niches 18721750.

Compound.name: a (2 R )-2-hydroxy even numbered straight chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acid
Comment: This class holds the R -enantiomer of 2-hydroxy, unbranched, 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids.

Compound.name: a pyrimidine nucleotide
Comment: A pyrimidine nucleotide is composed of |FRAME: Pyrimidine-Bases|, a five-carbon sugar (either |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose| or |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|), and one to three phosphate groups. When joined together, nucleotides make up the structural units of RNA and DNA. The nucleotides are called |FRAME: Ribonucleotides| when the sugar is |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose|, and |FRAME: Deoxynucleotides| when it is |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|.

Compound.name: a steroidal estrogen
Comment: Estrogens are hormones that stimulate or control the development and maintenance of female sex characteristics in mammals by binding to estrogen receptors. They are important in both the menstrual and the estrous reproductive cycles. Estrogens are synthesized in all vertebrates as well as some insects, suggesting that estrogenic sex hormones have an ancient evolutionary history. The estrogens that occur naturally in the body are steroids, however other types of molecules acquired in the diet are known to bind to the estrogen receptors and are thus also considered estrogens. They include molecules produced by plants (phytoestrogens), molecules produced by fungi (mycoestrogens), and synthetic compounds (xenoestrogens). The main steroidal |FRAME: Estrogens estrogens| in humans are |FRAME: ESTRONE|, |FRAME: CPD-352| and |FRAME: ESTRIOL|, which differ in the number of hydroxyl groups (one for |FRAME: ESTRONE|, two for |FRAME: CPD-352| and three for |FRAME: ESTRIOL|). |FRAME: CPD-352| is about 10 times as potent as |FRAME: ESTRONE| and about 80 times as potent as |FRAME: ESTRIOL| in its estrogenic effect. |FRAME: CPD-352| is the predominant estrogen in non-pregenant women during their reproductive years in terms of serum levels. |FRAME: ESTRONE Estrone| is the predominant circulating estrogen in women during menopause and |FRAME: ESTRIOL| is the predominant circulating estrogen during pregnancy.

Compound.name: D-arabinose
Comment: |FRAME: Arabinoses Arabinose| is an aldopentose - a monosaccharide containing five carbon atoms. Unlike many other aldoses, which are more abundant in nature as the "D"-form, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| is far more common in nature than |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|. Due to its scarcity, most microorganisms are not able to metabolize |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|. Compound.name: an opine
Comment: |FRAME: Opines Opines| are a large family of low molecular weight compounds. The vast majority of opines are secondary amine derivatives resulting from the reduction of the imine formed by condensation of an amino acid with either a keto acid or a sugar. Opines from the |FRAME: CPD-308| family are formed when |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| serves as the keto substrate in the condensation reaction, while those of the |FRAME: CPD-309| family are formed when |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is involved in the condensation reaction. Opines of the |FRAME: CPD-15773| and |FRAME: CPD-26410| families are formed by the condensation of an amino acid with a sugar. A small, separate class of opines is the |FRAME: Agrocinopines agrocinopines|, which are sugar-phosphodiesters (e.g., |FRAME: CPD-15774|, which is a phosphodiester of sucrose and L-arabinose). While opines are found in marine invertebrates, fungi, higher plants and mammals, they are most commonly found in plant crown gall tumors or hairy root tumors, where they are produced by bacteria of the genera |FRAME: TAX-357| and |FRAME: TAX-379|, respectively. However, the first opine to be identified (in 1927), octopine, was isolated from an octopus muscle, hence its name, which was later extended for naming the opine family. Biosynthesis of opines in crown gall tumors is performed by enzymes encoded by genes contained in T-DNA (transfer DNA), which is part of the Ti plasmid (in |FRAME: TAX-357|) or Ri plasmid (in |FRAME: TAX-379|). The plasmids are inserted by the bacteria into the plant genome, where they are integrated and expressed. Those opines are used by the bacteria as energy, carbon and nitrogen sources. Each strain of |FRAME: TAX-357| and |FRAME: TAX-379| induces and catabolizes a specific set of opines, determined by the specific Ti or Ri plasmid they possess, and Ti-plasmids are classified as nopaline-type, octopine-type, agropine-type, vitopine-type, succinamopine-type, and chrysopine-type 31386108. Over 30 different opines have been described.

Compound.name: a 7,8-dihydropterin

Compound.name: a long-chain alkane

Compound.name: a porphyrin
Comment: The porphyrins are a class of heterocyclic macrocycles derived from |FRAME: CPD-26422|, a molecule that consists of four |FRAME: Pyrroles pyrrole| rings joined together by four methine (=CH-) groups to form a larger macrocycle ring. Many porphyrins occur in nature, and fulfil important biochemical roles. Porphyrins can bind metals to form complexes. The metal ion, usually with a charge of 2+ or 3+, resides in the central cavity formed by the loss of two protons. Many metals are found within different derivatives, including Fe, Mg, Ni, Co and Zn. The name porphyrin comes from a Greek word for purple, since most porphyrins are red to purple in color. More reduced porphyrins, such as |FRAME: Corphins corphins|, are yellowish.

Compound.name: a [cullin]-L-lysine
Comment: |FRAME: Cullins Cullins| are a family of proteins that provide a scaffold for some RING-type E3 ubiquitin transferases (|FRAME: EC-2.3.2.27 "EC 2.3.2.27"|), which are not able to bind a substrate protein directly. These E3 proteins form a complex with a cullin protein and a substrate recognition subunit (SRS). Some complexes also include an adaptor that links the SRS to the complex. The complexes are known as CRLs for Cullin-RING ubiquitin Ligases. CRLs comprise the largest known category of ubiquitin ligases, and regulate an extensive number of dynamic cellular processes, including multiple aspects of the cell cycle, transcription, signal transduction, and development 18282298. There are five major types of cullins in metazoa, each of which forms a distinct class of CRL complex, with distinct adaptors and/or substrate-recognition subunits. CRLs are activated by the covalent attachment of the ubiquitin-like protein |FRAME: NEDD8 NEDD8| to the cullin, and are inhibited by binding to the CAND1 inhibitor 15688063. The human genome contains eight cullin genes.

Compound.name: a sialyl-Lewis a epitope
Synonyms: an sLe a antigen // alphaNeuNAc-(2->3)-betaGal-(1->3)-[alphaFuc-(1->4]-betaGlcNAc-[protein] // a histo-blood group sialyl Lewis a epitope
Comment: The |FRAME: sLea-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis a epitope"| (SLe a ) was discovered in 1979 with the use of a monoclonal antibody 94699. While the antigen is believed to play an important role during embryogenesis 6381330, in adults only low amounts of the antigen are present on normal epithelial cells |CITS: [6751528][6381289]|. When the selectin family of adhesion molecules was described, it was found that SLe a , along with the |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x antigen"|, is a ligand for E-selectin. Higher expression of the SLe a antigen in adults is strongly associated with cancer. It was found in high amounts on the surface of human pancreatic, colon and gastric cancer cell lines |CITS: [7142214][6188455]| and in human adenocarcinomas of the colon, stomach, pancreas and gall-bladder |CITS: [94699][6751528][2910493]|. The expression of the antigen has been linked to tumor progression. A gradual increase in SLe a was found in colon and rectum during neoplastic transformation and progression 2863413, and its presence was restricted to tumorigenic and invasive human urothelial cell lines 8900435. The antigen is responsible for adhesion of colon, pancreas, urinary bladder and gastric cancer cells to endothelium via its interaction with selectin E |CITS: [1716885][7687590][7678075][8900435][9578490]|. The expression level of the SLe a antigen is used as a prognostic factor for colorectal carcinoma, and is associated with high incidence of recurrence and the length of survival time |CITS: [8273774][7697593][9303355]|.

Compound.name: a B vitamin
Comment: B vitamins are a class of eight water-soluble vitamins that play important roles in cell metabolism. The B vitamins were classified together because all of them serve as either enzyme cofactors, cosubstrates in important metabolic reactions, or as precursors for cofactors or cosubstrates. The different B vitamins are chemically distinct compounds that do not resemble one another. The dietary supplements known as "B complexes" contain all eight of these compounds. The eight members of the vitamin B class are: Vitamin B 1 : |FRAME: THIAMINE| Vitamin B 2 : |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN| Vitamin B 3 : |FRAME: NIACINE|, |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE|, and |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_RIBOSE "nicotinamide riboside"| Vitamin B 5 : |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE| Vitamin B 6 : |FRAME: PYRIDOXINE|, |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL|, and |FRAME: PYRIDOXAMINE| Vitamin B 7 : |FRAME: BIOTIN| Vitamin B 9 : |FRAME: THF folate| Vitamin B 12 : |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| (although supplements usually contain |FRAME: CPD-9037| or |FRAME: CPD-315|, which are converted to the active form in vivo )

Compound.name: a fructan
Comment: Fructans are a class of highly water-soluble polysaccharides consisting of linear or branched FRU chains attached to |FRAME: SUCROSE| by beta-2,1or beta-2,6-linkage. There are 3 types of fructans: 1. |FRAME: Inulin| - linear fructans generally linked by beta(2->1) glycosidic bonds 2. |FRAME: Levan| - linear fructans generally linked by beta(2->6) glycosidic bonds 3. |FRAME: Graminans| - branched fructans linked by both beta(2->1) and beta(2->6) glycosidic bonds. The fructosyl units may be linked to the sucrose base unit either to the fructose moiety, or to the glucose moiety by a beta 2->6 bond. In the latter case, the resulting molecule name is marked by a 6 G , as in |FRAME: NEOKESTOSE 6 G -kestotriose|.

Compound.name: a di-homo-gamma-linolenate-derived metabolite
Comment: The oxidation of the polyunsaturated fatty acids |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-8120|, |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|, |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID|, |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE icosapentaenoate| (EPA) and |FRAME: CPD-10244 docosahexaenoate| (DHA) results a wide array of lipid metabolites, including (but not limited to) |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins|, |FRAME: Thromboxanes thromboxanes|, |FRAME: Leukotrienes leukotrienes|, |FRAME: Lipoxins lipoxins|, |FRAME: Resolvins resolvins|, and |FRAME: Eoxins eoxins|. The best-studied of these are the compounds derived from C20 acids, which are known as |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids|. Many of these compounds act as signaling molecules that play prominent roles in many physiological processes. In mammals they participate in the regulation of many key biological processes in the cardiovascular, renal, reproductive and other systems, with a particular important role in inflammation.

Compound.name: a ubiquinol
Synonyms: a reduced ubiquinone // a dihydroubiquinone // a QH 2

Their structures have a variable length side chain, which consists of one to twelve mono-unsaturated trans -isoprenoids units, with ten units being the most common in animals. |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 units, |FRAME: TAX-303| has 7, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, |FRAME: TAX-10090| has 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10 16233343. The terms ubiquinone/ubiquinol refer to the oxidized/reduced forms, and are often used interchangeably. The forms are readily interconvertable. Ubiquinone is also known as coenzyme Q, or just Q. The names are often followed by the number of the prenoid units in the side chain (e.g. Q-8), or the number of carbons in the chain. For example, the name Q-8 may be substituted with ubiiquinone(40). Since these carbons occur in repeating units of five, these number are multiples of 5.

Compound.name: a rhodoquinone
Comment: Rhodoquinone (RQ) is a modified ubiquinone, where the methoxyl group in position 3 is replaced by an amino group. The compound was originally isolated from TAX-1085 |CITS:[Glover62][14293762] [14285535]|, where is it used for the reduction of fumarate to succinate under anaerobic conditions. Rhodoquinone is not limited to prokaryotes. It was soon discovered that some eukaryotic parasites such as the nematodes |FRAME: TAX-6253| and |FRAME: TAX-6252| |CITS: [5796154][811785]|, as well as parasitic helminths 4795616 also contain rhodoquinone, which is essential for fumarate reduction under anaerobic conditions 2843227. Later it was shown that rhodoquinone is present in all eukaryotes that reduce fumarate during anoxia, including freshwater snails, mussels, lugworms, and oysters 8537365.

Compound.name: a purine base
Comment: Nucleobases are the parts of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) that are involved in pairing of the two strands. The primary nucleobases are |FRAME: CYTOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: ADENINE| (found in both DNA and RNA), |FRAME: THYMINE| (found only in DNA) and |FRAME: URACIL| (found only in RNA), abbreviated as C, G, A, T, and U, respectively. There are many additional nucleobases, usually derived from the primary ones. Based on their structure, nucleobases are divided into |FRAME: Purines purines| and |FRAME: Pyrimidine-Bases pyrimidines|. Purines are heterocyclic aromatic compounds that contain a |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING| ring fused to an |FRAME: IMIDAZOLE-RING| ring. Two of the bases in nucleic acids, |FRAME: ADENINE| and |FRAME: GUANINE|, are purines.

This class describes |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"| that do not contain any double bonds in the 2, 3, and 4 positions. The compounds in this class are often classified by the length of their aliphatic chains. |FRAME: Short-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "Short-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of less than 6 carbons. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "Medium-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chain of 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 13-22 carbons. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-234-Saturated-FAs "Very-long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 23 carbons or longer.

This remarkable tensile strength, combined with elasticity, is achieved by the structure of the cell wall's main component, peptidoglycan (also known as "basal structure", "mucopeptide", "glycopeptide", "glycosaminopeptide" and "murein"). Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman's net. The net is made of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads consisting of alternating |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (GlcNAc) and |FRAME: CPD-19950| (MurNAc) sugars, which are held together by small elastic peptide crosslinks which are formed between the side-chains of the different strands, allowing the net to expand or shrink 10532377. The structure below shows a region of peptidoglycan consisting of two monomers with pentapeptide side chains. R1 and R2 refer to the parts of the polymer upstream and downstream. Many variations exist in regard to the composition of the side chain.

The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain (producing |FRAME: Octanoylated-domains|), and is then converted to lipoate by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-782|, resulting in |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein-N6-lipoyllysine|. |FRAME: CPLX0-782 "Lipoate synthase"| not only catalyzes the reaction, but is also the source of the two sulfur atoms.

If carbon-1 is placed at the top of the molecule, L-numbering proceeds clockwise, while D-numbering proceeds counter-clockwise. Both the 1D or 1L designations can be employed currently. To aid in following the transformations in inositol compounds in pathways, the structures of inositol stereoisomers in MetaCyc have been formatted to show carbon 1 at the top of the ring, with numbering proceeding clockwise. An exception is the structure of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, which is presented with carbon 3 at the top and counter-clockwise numbering. The reason is that carbon 3 of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| (which is based on L-numbering) matches the carbon-1 of 1D numbering, which is used for the various phosphorylated and otherwise modified forms, and by presenting the molecule in this way, it is much easier to show structural relationships in reactions and pathways (see for example |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL-1-KINASE-RXN "EC 2.7.1.64"|).

Quinones are conjugated but not aromatic. A classic example of a quinone is |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE|. Quinones are commonly named with a prefix that indicates the parent aromatic hydrocarbon (for example, "benzo-" for benzene, "naphtho-" for naphthalene, and "anthra-" for anthracene) with a "-quinone" suffix. Several types of quinones serve as electron acceptors in electron transport chains. Those quinones are usually prenylated with a lipid-soluble isoprenyl tail that anchors them in the membrane lipid bilayer. Quinones can carry two electrons, and when fully reduced they are referred to as |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinols|. The addition of a single H atom to a quinone results in formation of a free radical called |FRAME: Semiquinones|. Many quinone derivatives often have other biological activities, such as |FRAME: CPD-11501 "vitamin K"|.

Compound.name: a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster
Synonyms: Iron-sulfur (4Fe-4S) // a 4Fe-4S iron-sulfur cluster // a 4Fe-4S center // a 4Fe-4S cluster // a 4Fe-4S iron-sulfur center // a Fe 4 S 4 iron-sulfur center // a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur center // [4Fe-4S] // 4Fe-4S // [4Fe-4S] cluster // Fe 4 S 4 cluster
Comment: Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as cofactors of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential. In addition to their roles in electron t ransfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They can also act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression 16466637. In some cases iron-sulfur clusters serve as sources of sulfur in enzymatic reactions 29051382 (see below). [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters feature four iron ions and four sulfide ions placed at the vertices of a cubane-type structure. The Fe centers are typically further coordinated by cysteinyl ligands. Two main types of [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters are low-potential (bacterial-type) clusters and high-potential (HiPIP) clusters. The bacterial clusters shift between the oxidation states +1 and +2, while the HiPIP clusters shift between the oxidation states +2 and +3. In some enzymes the [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters bind substrates. For example, in radical SAM enzymes the cluster binds and reduces S-adenosylmethionine, generating a radical that interacts with the enzyme's substrate. In a few cases, as in |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.8|, the cluster serves as the source of sulfur atoms for a sulfuration reaction. In such cases the cluster needs to be reassembled before the enzyme can catalyze the next round.

Compound.name: a tetrahydrofolate
Synonyms: tetrahydropteroyl polyglutamate // THF(glu) n // H 4 PteGlu n // a tetrahydrofolate-glutamate // THF // THF polyglutamate
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for tetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Compound.name: a dolichol
Comment: |FRAME: DOLICHOL "Dolichol"| is the name given to a family of long-chain polyprenols that contain a varying number of cis -linked isoprene units, terminating with three isoprene units, two of which are trans -linked. The first (alpha) unit in dolichols is always saturated 11442630. Additional modifications are found. For example, dolichols from certain halobacteria contain an additional saturation in the terminal (omega) isoprene unit |CITS: [9363431][21091511]|. The length of dolichol molecules varies within a range in a species, and the range varies among species (reviewed in 9878760). In mammals dolichols are usually within the range of 80 to 105 carbons. Archaea prefer dolichols of 55-60 carbons. The main function of dolichols is to act as a membrane anchor for the formation of oligosaccharides, which are then transferred to certain asparagine residues within proteins through a modification process known as |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS "N-glycosylation"|. In eukaryotes dolichol is also involved in the transfer of some of the monosaccharides to the forming oligosaccharide. Dolichols are the major lipid component (14% by mass) of human substantia nigra |FRAME: CPD-12419| 15686500.

Compound.name: a glycoconjugate
Comment: Glycoconjugate is the general term used for carbohydrates that are covalently linked with other chemical species such as proteins, peptides, lipids and saccharides. Examples for glycoconjugates include |FRAME: Glycoconjugates glycoproteins|, glycopeptides, |FRAME: Peptidoglycans peptidoglycans|, |FRAME: Glycolipids glycolipids|, |FRAME: Glycosides glycosides| and |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|. Glycoconjugates are often involved in cell-cell interactions, cell-cell recognition, cell-matrix interactions, and detoxification processes.

Compound.name: an anthraquinone
Comment: Anthraquinone derivatives are found in microorganisms, fungi, plants, marine organisms, and insects. In higher plants, most anthraquinones occur as mono- or diglycosides. The yellow or red colored compounds have some commercial relevance as natural dyes. 1,8-dihydroxyanthraquinones serve as laxatives. In fungi and some higher plants (Leguminosae, Rhamnaceae, Polygonaceae, and Caesalpiniaceae), anthraquinones are biosynthesized via a polyketide pathway which comprises the successive condensation of acetyl CoA with 7 molecules of malonyl CoA to form an octa-alpha-keto-acyl chain, which is converted to the anthraquinone system via decarboxylation, cyclization, and aromatization.

Compound.name: a protopanaxadiol-type ginsenoside with a single glucosyl residue at position 20
Comment: |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053| (ginseng). They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD, containing hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20), |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT, containing hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20), and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|.

Compound.name: a C-nitro compound
Comment: This class contains compounds that have a nitro group (-NO2) attached to a carbon atom.

Compound.name: a spinosyn
Comment: The spinosyns (previously referred to as A83543 factors Kirst91 are macrolides produced by |FRAME: TAX-60894| , a bacterium isolated from soil collected in a sugar mill rum still Mertz90. Spinosyns comprise a tetracyclic macrolide containing forosamine and tri-methylated rhamnose sugars, with different degrees of methylation on the polyketide or deoxysugars. The two major forms, |FRAME: CPD-13385| and |FRAME: CPD-13386|, differ from each other by a single methyl substituent at position 6 of the polyketide. The spinosyns show potent insecticidal activities against many commercially significant species that cause extensive damage to crops and other plants. They also show activity against important external parasites of livestock, companion animals and humans. Spinosad, a combination of |FRAME: CPD-13385| and |FRAME: CPD-13386|, is marketed by Dow AgroSciences for control of agricultural insect pests. Spinosad is highly effective against target insects and has an excellent environmental and mammalian toxicological profile. A semisynthetic second-generation derivative, named spinetoram, has been developed as well |CITS: [Sparks98][19082588][20150928][32893433]|. The spinosyns act by disruption of neural functions, most likely via an alteration of nicotinic receptor function |CITS: [Salgado98][15518655][Orr09]|. Another class of spinosyns, butenyl-spinosyns (pogonins), are produced by |FRAME: TAX-333966| and contain butenoyl substitution at C-21 16179985.

Compound.name: a phenoxyl radical of a phenolic donor
a [protein]- N -phospho-L-histidine
Comment: This entry has been included to accommodate those protein-histidines for which the phosphorylation site has not been established.

Compound.name: a bacteriochlorophyll c
Comment: Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight Overmann92. Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10-30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics. The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "|, depending on the species. They all possess a hydroxyl group at the C3 1 position that allows them to chelate the Mg atom of a neighboring molecule and to interact with the C13-oxo carbonyl group of another neighboring pigment molecule, affording the self-aggregation |CITS: [16121276][19435848][22210764]|. In addition, all of these bacteriochlorophylls lack C-13 2 -methylcarboxyl side chains, which are found in all other (bacterio)chlorophylls but would interfere with the ability to form aggregates 16245042. Despite of their names, |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "| are actually chlorins rather than bacteriochlorins. All three are usually found with an unsaturated farnesyl tail rather than phytyl tails |CITS: [2350541][Borrego99]|, although exceptions have been reported. In chlorosomes of |FRAME: TAX-191412| (but not |FRAME: TAX-1106| |CITS: [Risch79][3442679]|) all three types of bacteriochlorophyll appear in several forms with different degrees of methylation at the C-8 2 and C-12 1 carbons |CITS: [12656478][14610639]|. The variety in methylation is depicted in the structure shown here by the R groups. In general, pimgents produced by cultures grown at lower light intensities are more highly methylated at the C-8 2 position than pigments produced by cells of the same organism grown at higher light intensities. Different methylation states result in different aggregation properties and light absorbance of the chlorosome, and thus methylation is used as an adaptation to altering envireonmental conditions. Most of the green sulfur bacteria growing in stratified lakes contain CPD-9093, and species containing |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "| are rarely found vanGemerden95. Some examples for bacteria that possess |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "| are the green sulfur bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1092| and |FRAME: TAX-1097| and the green filamentous bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1108|.

Compound.name: a deaminated amino group donor
Comment: |FRAME: Amine-Donors "An amino group donor"| is a compound that can donate an amino group to another compound in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes that belong to the |FRAME: EC-2.6.1 transaminase group"| (often called aminotransferases). Prior to donating the amino group the compound is |FRAME: Aminated-Amine-Donors| and after donating it the compound is |FRAME: Deaminated-Amine-Donors|. Since tranmination reactions are reversible, the distinction between an amino group donor and an amino group acceptor is not determined by the actual chemical entity, but by the role it plays in a particular reaction. However, some compounds, such as |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, are often used as amino group donors by the aminotransferases in reactions that are physiologically unidirectional. This particular entry is used when the identity of the amino group donor (or acceptor) is not known or cannot be defined.

Compound.name: an amide
Comment: Amides are derivatives of oxoacids in which an acidic hydroxy group has been replaced by an amino or substituted amino group. Most amide compounds fall under |FRAME: Carboxamides carboxamides|, where the nitrogen atom is bonded with a carbon atom. However, the term amide also refers to compounds where the nitrogen is bonded to a non-carbon atom (see for example |FRAME: Sulfonamides|).

Compound.name: a neurotransmitter
Comment: Neurotransmitters are endogenous compounds that are used to transmit information across the synapse between a neuron and another cell.

Compound.name: a cellodextrin
Comment: Cellodextrins are beta-1,4 linked glucose polymers of varying length (two or more glucose monomers) resulting from the breakdown of cellulose. During the degradation of glucose an endoglucanase first cuts the crystalline cellulose in an amorphous zone producing somewhat shorter glucans. Exoglucanases subsequently cleave these large insoluble chunks of cellulose into smaller, soluble cellodextrins which can be used by the cell. Common cellodextrins are cellotriose, cellotetraose, cellopentaose and cellohexaose.

Compound.name: a Lewis epitope
Comment: The Lewis blood group antigens, discovered in 1946, are biosynthetically and structurally related carbohydrate structures used as markers of cell differentiation and embryonic development, based on fucosylation carried by a number of fucosyltransferases. The system is named after Mrs. H. D. G. Lewis, in whose serum the first member of the family was discovered 20995492. However, the presence of the Lewis antigens is not limited to erytrocytes, and they are found in different tissues and organs. One of these fucosyltransferases, encoded by the |FRAME: HS10249| gene, is bifunctional and can fucosylate both the 3 and 4 positions of the penultimate sugar in the precursor disaccharide. The gene, also known as the Lewis gene, has a dominant allele (which was named Le) and a recessive non-functional allele (known as le). The alpha(1,4)-fucosyltransferase activity is only relevant when the substrates are derived from the |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 precursor disaccharide"|, as that position is already occupied in the |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2 disaccharide"|. The first Lewis antigens to be discovered were the |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a"| and |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Lewis b"| antigens, which are produced from |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 precursor disaccharides"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7832|). However, the alpha(1,3) fucosylation of the N -acetylglucosaminyl residue of |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R| leads to formation of several related antigens known as the |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x epitope"| (also known as SSEA-1, for stage-specific embryonic antigen 1), |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y epitope"|, and the |FRAME: sLea-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x epitope"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7831|).

Compound.name: a polar amino acid
Comment: This class stands for all of the polar amino acids. The class contains both alpha and non-alpha amino acids. Amino acids with polar side groups form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, and are classified as hydrophilic. Polar amino acids that have substituents carrying either negative or positive charges in aqueous solution at neutral pH are strongly hydrophilic.

Compound.name: a gamma-lactone
Comment: A |FRAME: Lactones "lactone"| is a cyclic ester, the product of condensation of an alcohol group and a carboxylate group within the same molecule. It is characterized by a closed ring consisting of two or more carbon atoms and a single oxygen atom, with a ketone group in one of the carbons adjacent to the ring oxygen. There are several types of lactones - |FRAME: Beta-lactones| contain 3 carbons in the ring, Gamma-lactones contains 4, Delta-lactones contains 5, and Epsilon-lactones contains 6 carbons.

Compound.name: a beta-D-glucuronide
Synonyms: an acceptor beta-D-glucuronoside // a beta-D-glucuronoside // a beta-D-glucosiduronate

Compound.name: a 1-phosphatidyl-1D-myo-inositol 3-phosphate
Comment: The phosphorylated derivatives of |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols "phosphatidylinositol"| (PtdIns), collectively called phosphoinositides (PIs), are eukaryotic cell membrane phospholipids whose inositol head group is phosphorylated at position D3, D4, or D5, singly or in all combinations, to yield seven PI metabolites. The seven phosphoinositides found in animals include: Phosphatidylinositol monophosphates: |FRAME: CPD-177|, |FRAME: CPD-1108| and |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-5-PHOSPHA|. Phosphatidylinositol bisphophosphates: |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-34-BISPH|, |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-35-BISPH|, and |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA|. Phosphatidylinositol trisphophosphate: |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL-345-TRIPHOSPHATE|.

Compound.name: a derivative of n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid
phosphatidylcholine-36:5
Comment: In this group of Phosphatidylcholines, the length of the two acyl chains, and the location and number of the double bonds varies. For each of the group members, the total number of carbon atoms in the two acyl chains adds up to 36, and the total number of double bonds in the two acyl groups adds up to 5.

Compound.name: a ceramide NP
Comment: The human skin outermost layer (the stratum corneum) contains 12 main types of free ceramides. Two nomenclature systems have been used for the description of these ceramides. The older numbering system is based on the chromatographic migration (ceramide 1 to ceramide 8) and chronological arrangement of their publication (from ceramide 9 and on). A newer system is based on the molecular structure |CITS: [8357845][7868984]|. In this system each ceramide type is named by two or three letters, where the front letter(s) designate the acyl chain: N (non-hydroxy fatty acid), A (alpha-hydroxy fatty acid), O (ω--hydroxy fatty acid, or EO (an ω-hydroxy fatty acid esterified to linoleic acid), and the last letter designates the sphingoid base: S (|FRAME: SPHINGOSINE|), dS (|FRAME: CPD-13612 sphinganine|), P (|FRAME: PHYTOSPINGOSINE|), or H (|FRAME: CPD-22027|). The 12 types of free stratum corneum ceramides are |FRAME: Ceramide-EOS| (ceramide 1), |FRAME: Ceramide-NS| (ceramide 2), |FRAME: Ceramide-NP| (ceramide 3), |FRAME: Ceramide-EOH| (ceramide 4), |FRAME: Ceramide-AS| (ceramide 5), |FRAME: Ceramide-AP| (ceramide 6), |FRAME: Ceramide-AH| (ceramide 7), |FRAME: Ceramide-NH| (ceramide 8), |FRAME: Ceramide-EOP| (ceramide 9), ,|FRAME: Ceramide-NdS| (ceramide 10), |FRAME: Ceramide-AdS| (ceramide 11), and |FRAME: Ceramide-EOdS| (ceramide 12) |CITS: [7868984][18329855][23954553]|. The four EO types, |FRAME: Ceramide-EOS|, |FRAME: Ceramide-EOH|, |FRAME: Ceramide-EOP|, and |FRAME: Ceramide-EOdS|, are also known as |FRAME: Linoleate-Acylceramides acylceramides|. The four O-type ceramides of the stratum corneum are not found among the free ceramides, as they form an ester-linkage via their ω-hydroxyl group to to glutamate residues of proteins in the cornified envelope 27432202.

Compound.name: an icosanoid
Comment: Icosanoids (often spelled eicosanoids) are signaling molecules generated by oxidation of 20-carbon fatty acids. Icosanoids participate in many cellular processes including promoting or inhibiting inflammation; responding to allergy, fever and other immune system challenges; regulating normal childbirth; contributing to the perception of pain; regulating cell growth; controlling blood pressure; and modulating the regional flow of blood to tissues. There are multiple subfamilies of icosanoids, the main of which are the |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins|, |FRAME: Thromboxanes thromboxanes|, |FRAME: Leukotrienes leukotrienes|, |FRAME: Lipoxins lipoxins|, |FRAME: Resolvins resolvins|, and |FRAME: Eoxins eoxins|. Each family can have up to 4 series of compounds, which are derived from the ω-3 fatty acid |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE|), the ω-6 fatty acids |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| [(5Z,8Z,11Z,14Z)-icosatetraenoate] and |FRAME: CPD-8120| [(8Z,11Z,14Z)-icosatrienoate], and the ω-9 fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-24529|, respectively.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-(7Z)-hexadecenoate
Comment: In higher plants, the double bond in (16:1) fatty acids is at position 7 8066133. This form has also been reported from a few bacteria, including the obligate anaerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1520| and the saprophytic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1377| |CITS: [14498314][5554109][6886674][12583708][23972938]|. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: CPD-17289| is hardly found as a free acid, and is usually found as either |FRAME: 7Z-hexadec-7-enoyl-ACPs "(7Z)-hexadec-7-enoyl-[acp]"| or |FRAME: CPD-17294 "incorporated into lipids"|.

Compound.name: a medium-chain fatty alcohol
Comment: Fatty alcohols are aliphatic |FRAME: Alcohols alcohols| consisting of a chain of 3 or more carbon atoms. They may be saturated or unsaturated and may be branched or unbranched. Many enzymes that act on |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, |FRAME: Fatty-Alcohols alcohols|, and |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes aldehydes|, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Alcohols "Short-chain alcohols"| have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Alcohols "Medium-chain alcohols"| have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-chain-alcohols "Long-chain alcohols"| have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Alcohols "Very-long-chain alcohols"| have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Alcohols "Ultra-long-chain alcohols"| have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain.

Compound.name: a reduced flavin
Comment: A |FRAME: FLAVIN flavin| is a chemical moiety found in the compounds |FRAME: FAD| and |FRAME: FMN|, both important redox cofactors involved in many important reactions in metabolism. Flavin can exist in two different redox states, which it converts between by accepting or donating electrons. The |FRAME: Oxidized-Flavins "fully oxidized form"| (or quinone form) accepts two electrons and two protons to become the |FRAME: Reduced-Flavins "fully reduced form"| (hydroquinone form). The reduced form can be oxidized to a semireduced form (semiquinone) by donating one electron and one proton. A second oxidation results in restoring the initial quinone form. The conjugated ring system of fully oxidized flavin confers a bright yellow color, and its name is derived from flavus , Latin for yellow. Flavins are synthesized from |FRAME: GTP| in the form of |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN|, which is later modified into |FRAME: FMN| or |FRAME: FAD|. Since mammals cannot synthesize |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN|, it is an essential vitamin for them.

Compound.name: an arabinogalactan
Comment: |FRAME: Arabinogalactan Arabinogalactans| are biopolymers consisting of arabinose and galactose residues. Two main classes of arabinogalactans are found in nature: |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans "plant arabinogalactan"| and |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "microbial arabinogalactan"|. |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans "Plant arabinogalactan"| is a major constituent of many gums, and a major component of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| of some plants. |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "Microbial arabinogalactan"| is a major structural component of the mycobacterial cell wall.

Compound.name: a glycosaminoglycan
Comment: Glycosaminoglycans (also known as mucopolysaccharides) are important components of connective tissues. They are composed of long unbranched polysaccharides consisting of a repeating disaccharide unit. The repeating units consist of an N -acetyl-hexosamine and a hexose or hexuronic acid, either or both of which are often sulfated. Members of the glycosaminoglycan family vary in the type of hexosamine, hexose or hexuronic acid unit they contain (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-12521|, |FRAME: CPD-12515|, galactose, CPD-12557, |FRAME: CPD-12541|). Glycosaminoglycans are divided into four main classes: |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|; |FRAME: HEPARIN| and |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate|; |FRAME: Hyaluronan|; and |FRAME: KERATAN-6-SULFATE "keratan sulfate"|. With the exception of hyaluronan, the polysaccharide chains are linked covalently at the reducing end to a core protein through an O -glycosidic linkage to a serine residue. The modified proteins are known as |FRAME: Proteoglycans proteoglycans|. Most glycosaminoglycans are attached via a specific tetrasaccharide known as the |FRAME: GlcA-Gal-Gal-Xyl-Proteins "glycosaminoglycan-protein linkage region"|.

Compound.name: a negatively-charged polar amino acid
Comment: This class stands for all of the negatively-charged polar amino acids. It contains both alpha and non-alpha amino acids.

Compound.name: mannuronate
Comment: |FRAME: Mannuronate Mannuronate| is a reducing acidic sugar that exists in solution in multiple configurations. It can form a ring structure, as shown for |FRAME: CPD-14490| and |FRAME: CPD-15205|. The open-chain structure shown here, which is the structure of |FRAME: CPD-21250|, is provided only as a schematic illustration of chirality. Consult the appropriate class instances for information on specific ring structures and their anomeric configuration.

Compound.name: a sugar
Comment: The term sugar is used as a generic name for sweet-tasting, soluble carbohydrates. The term is not a specific chemical definition, but is frequently applied to |FRAME: Monosaccharides monosaccharides| and lower |FRAME: Oligosaccharides oligosaccharides|.

Compound.name: a plastoquinone
Comment: |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE Plastoquinones| (PQ) are benzoquinone electron carriers that can function as acceptor/donor for either one or two electrons. They are analogs of |FRAME: Ubiquinones "ubiquinones"| (Coenzyme Q), with two methyl groups substituting the methoxy groups found in Q. The fully reduced form is called |FRAME: Plastoquinols|. Plastoquinones are found in the chloroplasts of higher plants, red, brown and green algae, and in cyanobacteria, and are important members of the photosynthetic electron transfer chain, where they carry electrons from |FRAME: CPLX490-3506| to the |FRAME: CPLX-9022|. In fact, it has been shown that in cyanobacteria essentially all electron transport through unbound quinones proceeds via PQ in cyanobacterial thylakoids. Apart from PQ the only quinone found in thylakoids is vitamin K1, which is associated with PS I Vermaas01. Plastoquinones also serve as cofactors involved in the desaturation of phytoene in the synthesis of carotenoids (see |FRAME: PWY-6475|). Plastoquinone was isolated originally in 1946 from alfalfa, but was not identified at the time. It was rediscovered in 1959 and its structure was described in the same year (see 7022156). Please note that tyhe structure shown here is that of |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE-9| and is not accurate for this generic class of compounds, which contains plastoquinones with different side-chain lengths.

Compound.name: a pyrimidine ribonucleoside
Comment: Nucleosides are glycosylamines consisting of |FRAME: Bases| bound to a |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose| or |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE| sugar via a beta-glycosidic linkage. The nucleosides are called |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| when the sugar is |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose|, and |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| when it is |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|. Common |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| include |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, |FRAME: URIDINE|, |FRAME: ADENOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANOSINE| and |FRAME: INOSINE|. Examples of |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| include |FRAME: THYMIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYADENOSINE|. When nucleosides are phosphorylated on the sugar's primary alcohol group, the resulting phosphonucleosides are called |FRAME: Nucleotides nucleotides|. Pyrimidine is a heterocyclic aromatic compound similar to benzene, containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. Comment: Strigolactones are plant hormones that stimulate the branching and growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but inhibit plant shoot branching. They promote the probability of establishment of a symbiotic association between the plant and the fungi. The first strigolactone (|FRAME: CPD-14655|) was described from |FRAME: TAX-3635| (cotton) infected by the root parasitic weeds |FRAME: TAX-4169| (witchweed) (hence the name). It has been shown that the seeds of the parasites germinated only if they were exposed to stimulant molecules present in the root exudate of the host. Although the nature of strigol was not understood at the time, it was observed that it was active at hormonal levels 17780042. Discovery of additional strigolactones from other plants followed, such as |FRAME: CPD-14659| from |FRAME: TAX-4558| Hauck92, |FRAME: CPD-14660| from |FRAME: TAX-3917| Mueler92 and |FRAME: CPD-14657| from |FRAME: TAX-57577| (red clover) Yokota98. The real purpose of strigolactones, which was understood 40 years after the discovery of strigol, is to promote the formation of symbiotic associations known as arbuscular mycorrhiza, which consist of close interaction between the plants roots and |FRAME: TAX-214504| fungi |CITS: [15944706][16574693]|. Arbuscular mycorrhiza, which are found in more than 80% of higher plant species, are one of the most ancient symbioses of land plants. The fungi acquire and deliver nutrients to the plants, which in return provides the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis 15944687. The lactones induce extensive hyphal branching in germinating spores of the fungi, which increases the chance of contact with the root and subsequently infecting it. The branching phenomenon has been known for more than 30 years before the identity of the chemical signal that promotes it has been traced to strigolactone Mosse73. Since strigolactones are very labile and active at concentrations as low as picomolar, they are active only in close proximity to potential host roots, ensuring successful interactionbetween the fungi the roots. Study of mutants lacking strigolactones suggest that the hormones are also involved in the regulation of shoot branching, acting as branch-inhibiting hormones |CITS: [15268852][15342640]|.

Comment: The |FRAME: Furanocoumarins furanocoumarins| are one of the main groups of coumarins. Furanocoumarins are minor constituents in plants belonging to |FRAME: TAX-4037|, |FRAME: TAX-3803|, |FRAME: TAX-3487|, and |FRAME: TAX-23513| families. They are natural toxins that protect the plants from insects, herbivory, and microbes. Production is triggered by several types of stresses, including fungal infections |CITS: [6682038][8062387]| and stresses such as wounding Zangerl90 or acid fog Dercks90 . Furanocoumarins are also toxic to humans. Direct contact with the sap from some plants containing furanocoumarins (such as |FRAME: TAX-380077|) causes inflammation, burns and irritating sensitivity to sunlight 33174568. Some naturally occurring methoxy derivatives of furanocoumarins have been applied clinically, coupled with exposure to sunlight, to cure dermatological diseases for more than 2000 years. Linear furanocoumarins such as |FRAME: CPD-13042| and |FRAME: 5-METHOXYFURANOCOUMARIN| are used in the clinic in combination with UV radiation to treat several diseases, such as mycosis fungoides, vitiligo and psoriasis. Several clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate furanocoumarins potential to treat additional conditions, such as graft versus host disease, Crohn's disease, and several cancer types 33174568. A well documented toxicity of furanocoumarins is related to their inhibition of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes 14769198. An example is the interaction of furanocoumarins produced by grapefruit with |FRAME: HS08544-MONOMER| (CYP3A4), an enzyme that is involved in the bioinactivation of about 50% of all drugs currently used, resulting in enhanced systemic drug concentration through impaired drug metabolism, and leading to recommendation to avoid grapefruit while taking drugs 23184849.

It is typically more concentrated in plant systems than in animals, forming 1.5-4·5% of the lipid fraction |CITS: [23532185][3592680]| Since its discovery, biochemical research into PG has been dominated by its roles in the surfactant of lung tissue (PG is the second largest lipid constituent of lung surfactant in almost all mammals), chloroplast membranes (PG is the only phospholipid found in chloroplast thylakoids) and in both bacterial and mammalian systems.

The estrogens that occur naturally in the body are steroids, however other types of molecules acquired in the diet are known to bind to the estrogen receptors and are thus also considered estrogens. Comment: Cardiac glycosides are plant-made compounds (mostly by members of the |FRAME: TAX-4163| genus, or Foxgloves) that have beneficial effects over patients with cardiac failure. The treatment of congestive heart failure (dropsy), among other ailments like tuberculosis, by the use of Foxglove is mentioned in writings as early as 1250 A. D., when the Welsh Physicians of Myddva collected foxglove as one of their many herbs and included it in their remedies. 28561136. The cardiac glycosides are composed of two structural features: a sugar moiety that may contain one or more saccharides, and a steroid aglycone. Cardiac glycosides having a terminal glucose are called primary glycosides whereas those lacking such a sugar are termed secondary glycosides. There are two classes of cardiac glycosides differing by the group attached at the 17-position of the aglycone: the |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolides"|, which have a five-membered unsaturated lactone ring (but-2-en-4-olide ring) and the |FRAME: Bufadienolide-Glycosides bufadienolides|, which have a six membered doubly unsaturated lactone ring (penta-2,4-dien-5-olide ring). The steroid nucleus of the cardiac glycosides have a unique configuration: rings A/B and C/D are cis - fused while rings B/C are trans - fused. The nucleus has beta configured hydroxyls at the positions C-3 and C-14, and many compounds have additional hydroxyl groups at positions 12 and 16. The sugars found in the glycoside moiety range from common hexoses and pentoses (such as |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-Xylose|) to very uncommon sugars, some of which have only been found in cardiac glycosides (e.g. |FRAME: D-quinovopyranose|, |FRAME: CPD-22597|, |FRAME: D-Digitoxose|, |FRAME: CPD-22572|, |FRAME: D-Olivose|, and |FRAME: D-Fucoses|). While the mechanism whereby cardiac glycosides cause a positive inotropic effect and electrophysiologic changes of the hurt is still not completely clear, the most widely accepted mechanism involves the ability of cardiac glycosides to inhibit the membrane bound Na+/K+-ATPase pump responsible for Na+/K+ exchange KAUTE08.

Compound.name: NAD(P) +
Comment: |FRAME: NAD-P-OR-NOP| is a class of compounds including the instances |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP|. |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). They are often referred to as coenzymes, although in most of their reactions they function as cosubstrates rather than true coenzymes. The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form. |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|).

The backbone of natural rubber comprises a ( cis )-1,4-polyisoprene with two or three trans -isoprene units at the ω-terminus, formed by the sequential condensation of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) units in cis configuration onto a short all-trans prenyl diphosphate. It is very similar in structure to |FRAME: DOLICHOL dolichols|, but the chain length is much longer (C>1500). Natural rubber is produced from latex - a material that makes up the cytoplasmic content of the latecifers or latex vessels of |FRAME: TAX-3981| (the Brazilian rubber tree) 17545224. Although over 2000 plant species capable of producing rubber have been identified, only a few synthesize the high molecular weight rubber that is required for the production of high quality rubber products, and natural rubber is currently produced commercially only from |FRAME: TAX-3981|. A potential alternative source is the Russian rubber-producing dandelion (|FRAME: TAX-333970|), which was cultivated in the former Soviet Union during World War II to satisfy the demand for natural rubber 22504822. Rubber biosynthesis is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.20|. The enzyme is localized at the surface of cytosolic vesicles known as rubber particles, and biosynthesis is initiated through the binding of an allylic pyrophosphate primer, such as |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| |CITS: [Tanaka01][14622254][18799172]|. The R in the structure stands for an unspecified number of ( cis )-connected isoprene units.

Compound.name: dopamine
Comment: Dopamine is an amine compound synthesized in plants and most animals. In the brain, dopamine functions as a neurotransmitter - a chemical released by neurons (nerve cells) to send signals to other nerve cells. Outside the central nervous system, dopamine functions primarily as a local paracrine messenger. In blood vessels, it inhibits norepinephrine release and acts as a vasodilator (at normal concentrations); in the kidneys, it increases sodium excretion and urine output; in the pancreas, it reduces insulin production; in the digestive system, it reduces gastrointestinal motility and protects intestinal mucosa; and in the immune system, it reduces the activity of lymphocytes. With the exception of the blood vessels, dopamine in each of these peripheral systems is synthesized locally and exerts its effects near the cells that release it. Many plants synthesize dopamine, with the highest concentrations observed in bananas. The functions of plant catecholamines have not been clearly established, but there is evidence that they play a role in the response to stressors such as bacterial infection, act as growth-promoting factors in some situations, and modify the way that sugars are metabolized. Dopamine has been detected in some types of bacteria, and homologs of all the enzymes used by animals to synthesize dopamine have been detected in some bacteria.

Compound.name: NADPH
Synonyms: reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate // NADPH2 // NADPH 2 // dihydrotriphosphopyridine nucleotide // reduced dihydrotriphosphopyridine nucleotide // dihydronicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate // dihydronicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate reduced // reduced NADP // NADP-red // TPNH // dihydronicotinamide adenine dinucleotide-P // beta-NADPH // beta-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate, reduced
Comment: |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as |FRAME: Cofactors cofactors|. They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes". The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form. |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|).

Comment: |FRAME: THIAMINE Thiamin(e)|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. Compound.name: vinblastine
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-7858 Vinblastine| is a bisindole alkaloid produced by the plant |FRAME: TAX-4058| (Madagascar periwinkle). It is used as a chemotherapy medication, typically with other medications, to treat a number of types of cancer, including Hodgkin's lymphoma, non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer, brain cancer, melanoma, and testicular cancer. Its anticancer activity is a result of its binding to tubulin, thereby inhibiting the assembly of microtubules, resulting in cell cycle arrest. The anti-proliferative properties of |FRAME: CPD-7858| were discovered by serendipity. A tea made from |FRAME: TAX-4058| has been used for a long time as a folk-remedy for diabetes. When the tea was tested in a lab in 1949, it failed to show any effect on diabetes. However, when the extract was injected into rats, they died within a few days from a bacterial infection. Further research has found that administering the extract by injection resulted in a severely reduced white blood cell count and bone marrow depression. An effort to identify the active compound started in 1955, and partially enriched material was shown to possess carcinostatic activity against transplantable mammary adenocarcinoma 13627916. The structure of the compound, originally named vincaleukoblastine, was reported in 1958 Noble58, and its anticancer effects were confirmed shortly after |CITS: [13719013][13842983][14407465]|.

Comment: |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as |FRAME: Cofactors cofactors|. They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes". The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form. |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|).

Comment: Bilirubin is a yellow compound that is produced in vertebrates during heme degradation and is excreted in bile and urine. During the degradation the porphyrin ring of heme is broken, so bilirubin consists of an open chain of four pyrrole-like rings. Several enzymes that cleave the heme ring exist, cleaving it at different positions and generating different bilirubin compounds. The most common enzyme, which is also found in mammals, produces |FRAME: BILIRUBIN|. The structure of bilirubin-IX alpha was originally established by Hans Fischer in 1941, who did not specify the isomeric configuration Fischer41. It was later shown that the naturally occurring form of bilirubin is the |FRAME: BILIRUBIN " Z,Z isomer"| Lemberg49. However, when exposed to light, the Z,Z isomer converts to an |FRAME: CPD-20930 E,E isomer"|. Unconjugated bilirubin is extremely water insoluble. It is carried (mostly by albumin) to the liver, where it is converted to glucuronides, which are water soluble. The glucuronides are eventually excreted in bile. Glucuronated forms include both monoglucuronides (a mixture of the two positional isomers |FRAME: CPD-20932| and |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-GLUCURONOSIDE|) and |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-BISGLUCURONOSIDE| |CITS: [5145912][949313][7378044]|. Four basic forms of bilirubin are found in blood: |FRAME: BILIRUBIN "unconjugated bilirubin"| (alpha bilirubin), |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-GLUCURONOSIDE "mono-conjugated"| (beta bilirubin), |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-BISGLUCURONOSIDE "di-conjugated"| (gamma bilirubin), and protein bound (delta bilirubin) 5902889.

Compound.name: ergothioneine (thione form)
Comment: |FRAME: Ergothioneine Ergothioneine| (EGT) is a histidine derivative with a thiol group attached to the C2 atom of the imidazole ring and a trimethylated amine. EGT was initially isolated in 1909 by Tanret from |FRAME: TAX-5111| (ergot), the fungal infection of rye grain Tanret09, and its structure was determined within two years Barger11. It has been reported only from certain fungi, actinomycetales bacteria and cyanobacteria |CITS: [13376573][13405916][Pfeiffer11]|. The function of EGT in the microbial cells is not well understood, even though it is believed that EGT may protect cells from oxidative stress |CITS: [Garay56][2172707][22001064]|. The most significant difference between EGT and other biological thiols is the instability of the EGT disulfide under physiological conditions. Unlike other small thiols such as |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|, EGT is stable in its reduced form in aerated aqueous solutions and does not form the disulfide 15730267. Another significant difference is that EGT exists predominantly as the |FRAME: Ergothioneine-Thione "thione form"| at physiological pH 22001064. Although EGT is not synthesized by non-fungal eukaryotes, animals and plants acquire EGT from the environment through a specific transporter, ETT/OCTN1 15795384. It has been shown that the human body absorbs it from dietary sources and concentrates it in specific tissues or cells such as liver, kidney, central nervous system, and red blood cells 2172707. Both hyperactivity and deficiency of the OCTN1 transporter exert negative effects on human cells |CITS: [15795384][19136526]|. The precise function of ergothioneine in human tissue is also uncertain 17616140.

Comment: |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE "Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate"| (PLP, vitamin B6) is an essential cofactor in all living systems 7748903. It is one of the most versatile cofactors and participates in transamination, decarboxylation, racemization, Calpha-Cbeta cleavage and alpha-beta elimination reactions. PLP plays an important role in amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism and has been implicated in singlet oxygen resistance 10687384. In most enzymes the aldehyde group of PLP forms a Schiff-base linkage (internal aldimine) with the epsilon-amino group of a specific lysine residue at the active site. An amino group of the substrate displaces the epsilon-amino group of the active-site lysine residue in a process known as transaldimination. The resulting external aldimine can lose a proton, carbon dioxide, or an amino acid sidechain to become a quinonoid intermediate, which in turn can act as a nucleophile in several reaction pathways. It should be noted that while this is the most common mechanisms, exceptions do occur - for example, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.1|, which utilizes the phosphate group on PLP to perform its reaction, and |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.168|, which has a histidine instead of a lysine in the active site and converts PLP to the |FRAME: PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| (PMP) form. Most bacteria, archaea, fungi, and plants synthesize PLP de novo in a single reaction, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6466|. Some bacteria use a longer, more complex pathway (see |FRAME: PYRIDOXSYN-PWY|). However, PLP is often synthesized by salvage pathways.

Most of the bacteria that synthesize bacteriochlorophyll are anoxygenic species that belong to the proteobacteria. They are also known as purple bacteria, due to the color of the pigment. As of 2021, no biosynthetic pathway for usnic acid has been described. A usnic acid biosynthetic gene cluster from the lichen |FRAME: TAX-174080| was proposed in 2016 26895859. A putative polyketide synthase gene involved in usnic acid biosynthesis has been described from the lichen |FRAME: TAX-150890| in 2018 30020937. Compound.name: arsenite
Comment: Arsenic is the most prevalent environmental toxic substance. It ranks first on the priority list of Hazardous Substances published by the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR), based on a combination of frequency, toxicity, and potential for human exposure. It is also a Group 1 human carcinogen associated with skin, bladder and lung cancer. While arsenic exists in two oxidation states, As III and As V , in aerobic environments most inorganic arsenic is found as As(V), such as |FRAME: ARSENATE|. In anaerobic environments the prevalent form is As(III), such as |FRAME: CPD0-2040|. While most of the literature refers to the As(III) form found in the environment as |FRAME: CPD-763|, at natural pH values most of the As III molecules exist in solution as |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, an inorganic polyol similar to glycerol, since the pKa values are high: pKa 1 = 9:2 and pKa 2 = 12:7 |CITS: [11161507][15106984]|. This form of arsenite can enter cells via glycerol channels such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| or aquaglyceroporins, bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules such as glycerol to pass through. Charged forms of arsenite, formed at higher pH, include |FRAME: CPD-763 "arsenite 1- "|, |FRAME: CPD-24319| and |FRAME: CPD-24318|.

Compound.name: L-mimosine
Comment: |FRAME: MIMOSINE|, beta-(3-hydroxy-4-pyridon-1-yl)-L-alanine, is a non-protein amino acid found in the legume species |FRAME: TAX-76306| and |FRAME: TAX-3866|. It acts as an iron chelator and blocks the mammalian cell cycle at the G1/S phase. Mimosine suppresses the synthesis of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3a (eIF3a or eIF p170) and, subsequently, retards the translation of alpha-tubulin Dong04 and ribonucleotide reductase 12972576. Chelation of zinc by mimosine is also suggested to affect the function of zinc finger transcription factors, which impede the transcription of cytoplasmic serine hydroxymethyltransferase (cSHMT), an essential enzyme for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis 15531579. |FRAME: TAX-3866| is wide-spread in tropical and subtropical agricultural systems and provides a ready source of protein for livestock. Ruminants from Australia and India are unable to metabolize |FRAME: MIMOSINE| to non-toxic components, but ruminants in Hawaii and Indonesia can consume diets rich in Leucaena without showing any ill effects, due to rapid bacterial degradation of |FRAME: MIMOSINE| in the rumen |CITS: [Megarrity83][Allison92][7871781][7900214][7665380][Pandey07]|. Rumen fluid from Hawaiian goats has been successfully transferred to Australian ruminants to overcome the toxicity of |FRAME: TAX-3866| 3790013.

Within the two subtribes Diocleinae and Erythrininae it was found in 12 species representing 4 genera Ingham90. Maackiain was originally discovered in the |FRAME: TAX-37501| tree 13918216, which is named after its discoverer, the 19th-century Siberian explorer Karlovich Maack. Maackiain can be found in both a (-) and a (+) conformations. In chickpea, where it is a major pterocarpan phytoalexin together with medicarpin, it occurs exclusively in the (-) [(6aR,11aR)} conformation 8071365. |FRAME: CPD-3631 "(-)-Maackiain"| was reported to possess antiallergic properties, alleviating nasal symptoms through the inhibition of H1R (histamine H1 receptor) and IL-4 (interleukin-4) gene expression 26516579.

It is a cyclic compound made of three units of 2,3-dihydroxybenzoylserine joined in a cyclic structure by lactone linkages (only the delta-cis isomer of the ferric chelate is biologically active). |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN Enterobactin| binds Fe 3+ with a estimated Kd of 10 -49 M (10 -35 M at physiological pH) 16076215. |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN Enterobactin| not only is used by the organisms that produce it but also serves as an exosiderophore for many bacteria that are unable to synthesize it, such as |FRAME: TAX-287|, in a strategy of siderophore piracy |CITS: [26431675][30086222]|.
