Comment: |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| (FPP) has been recognized as a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of more complex sesquiterpenoids, higher terpenoids, and steroids for many years, and more recently many other roles have been discovered for both the pyrophosphate form and the corresponding alcohol farnesol. For example, farnesol acts as a quorum-sensing molecule to suppress filamentation in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5476| 12954333, and farnesyl derivatives are involved in the a-factor mating peptide of the dodecapeptide pheromone found in |FRAME: TAX-4932| 11112575. Terpene alcohols such as farnesol have antibacterial effects against |FRAME: TAX-1280|, including promotion of potassium ion leakage 15321680. Furthermore, FPP plays a pivotal role in the posttranslational processing of Ras proteins. Farnesol has 4 isomers, the most abundant of which is 2-TRANS6-TRANS-FARNESOL Yu05.

Compound.name: alpha,alpha-trehalose
Comment: The name trehalose was introduced in 1858 to describe a main constituent of shells that are secreted by various insects on tree leaves in the middle east. These shells were often dried and used as a sweetening agents, and are believed to be related to the biblical Manna, the food supplied to the Israelites in their journey through the wilderness of Arabia. One variety of these shells, produced by some beetles from the |FRAME: TAX-202007| genus ( Larinus maculatus and Larinus nidificans ) was called "trehala manna", and the sugar extracted from it was named trehalique glucose, or trehalose 12065209. In fact, |FRAME: TREHALOSE| is a disaccharide that is ubiquitous in the biosphere. It consists of two subunits of glucose bound by their reducing ends in an alpha:1-1 linkage (alpha-D-glucopyranosyl alpha-D-glucopyranoside) and thus does not have a reducing end. Trehalose has been isolated and characterized from many prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, including bacteria, yeast, plants, insects and mammals 11081789. In addition to being nonreducing, trehalose possesses several unique properties, including high hydrophilicity, chemical stability, nonhygroscopic glass formation and no internal hydrogen bond formation. The combination of these features explains the principal role of trehalose as a stress metabolite. In prokaryotic organisms trehalose can be used as external carbon source 7651129, a compatible solute (in cyanobacteria and photosynthetic bacteria) 8480996, a stress protector 8391102, and a structural component (part of the cord factor in mycobacteria) 8075141. In yeast and filamentous fungi, the main roles of trehalose are as a carbohydrate storage 6325857 and as a stress protector 7887593. The enzymes for trehalose metabolism are present in higher animals, but their precise role is not well understood 11081789.

Synonyms: MoO 2 -Mo-MPT // MoO 2 Dtpp-mP // {[(5aR,8R,9aR)-2-amino-4-oxo-6,7-di(sulfanyl-κ S )-1,5,5a,8,9a,10-hexahydro-4H-pyrano[3,2-g]pteridin-8-yl]methyl dihydrogenato(2-) phosphate}(dioxo)molybdate // MoO 2 -molybdopterin cofactor // MoO 2 (OH)Dtpp-mP // MoO 2 (OH)-MPT // MoCo (dioxyo) // molybdenum cofactor (dioxyo)
Comment: The transition element molybdenum is an essential micronutrient for microorganisms, plants, and animals. Molybdenum itself is catalytically inactive and needs to be complexed by a special cofactor to gain catalytic activity. It is bound to a unique pterin (molybdopterin, or MPT), forming the molybdenum cofactor, often referred to as MoCo 23539623. The MoCo form that is synthesized initially is |FRAME: CPD-15870|. In eukaryotes this form is incorporated into enzymes as-is, or undergoes sulfurylation as described in |FRAME: PWY-5963|. However, in prokaryotes the initial form is modified into many different forms. For example, enzymes of the xanthine oxidase family utilize |FRAME: CPD-23445| (MCD), while enzymes of the DMSO reductase family utilize |FRAME: CPD-15873| (bis-MGD) 21528011.

Where in |FRAME: CPD-11444| the side chains of all four rings have the same relative positions, in |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| the order is reversed on one of the rings. While |FRAME: CPD-11444| can be formed spontaneously from |FRAME: HYDROXYMETHYLBILANE|, the formation of |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| requires a dedicated enzyme - |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.75 "EC 4.2.1.75, uroporphyrinogen-III synthase"|. Both isomers are substrates for |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.37 "EC 4.1.1.37, uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase"|, although |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| is a better substrate 6724109.

Compound.name: FAD

Comment: |FRAME: FAD "Flavin adenine dinucleotide"| (FAD) is an important redox cofactor involved in many reactions in metabolism. The fully oxidized form, FAD, is converted to the reduced form, |FRAME: FADH2| by receiving two electrons and two protons. The reduced form can be oxidized to a |FRAME: FADH "semireduced form"| (semiquinone, FADH) by donating one electron and one proton. The semiquinone is then oxidized back to the fully oxidized form by losing a second electron and proton. Even though FAD has an aromatic ring system, FADH2 does not, making it significantly higher in energy. Many proteins contain a flavin moiety, either in the form of FAD or |FRAME: FMN|. They are known as |FRAME: Flavoproteins flavoproteins|.

Compound.name: tetrahydromethanopterin
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-10763 Methanopterin| is one of several modified folates that have been identified in Archaea |CITS: [6319137][2624671][1910453][1915350][8501071]| (see also |FRAME: CPD-10764|). While common in all methanogenic archaea, some C1-oxidizing members of the domain Bacteria also contain an |FRAME: THMPT|-related carrier, which they use in energy metabolism (see |FRAME: PWY-1723|). Serving a similar role to the one that folates serve in bacteria and eukaryotes, |FRAME: CPD-10763| carries C1 (single carbon) fragments between formyl and methyl oxidation levels (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|). Despite the similarities, there are clear differences between |FRAME: THF tetrahydrofolate| and |FRAME: THMPT|. In the reductive direction, ATP is consumed in the entry of carbon from |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| into the |FRAME: THF tetrahydrofolate| pathway, but not in entry into the |FRAME: THMPT| pathway. In the oxidative direction, methyl groups are much more readily oxidized on |FRAME: THMPT| than on |FRAME: THF tetrahydrofolate|. Moreover, the redox reactions on |FRAME: THMPT| are coupled to more negative reductants than the pyridine nucleotides which are used in the |FRAME: THF tetrahydrofolate| pathway 10970772.

Compound.name: 5-phospho-alpha-D-ribose 1-diphosphate

It is utilized in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: THMPT| in certain archaeal species and in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD1G-1531 "mycolyl-arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan complex"| in |FRAME: TAX-1773|. pRpp was discovered in the mid-1950s while searching for an enzyme that converted |FRAME: OROTATE| to |FRAME: UMP| |CITS: [14392173][13525411]|. The enzyme catalyzing the synthesis of pRpp, |FRAME: EC-2.7.6.1|, is ubiquitous among free-living organisms. So far, only certain obligate intracellular parasites such as some |FRAME: TAX-810| and |FRAME: TAX-780| species are known to lack the gene encoding it. Mammals contain three PRPP synthase-encoding genes, the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| contains five, and the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| contains five genes as well 28031352.

Thus the compound exists in several resonance structures. Imidazole also exists in two equivalent tautomeric forms, |FRAME: IMIDAZOLE-RING| and |FRAME: CPD-19703|. Different numbering systems have been used leading to confusion in the naming of imidazole compounds. When a side chain exists (as in L-histidine), the nitrogen atoms of the ring are denoted by pros ('near', abbreviated π) and tele ('far', abbreviated T) to show their position relative to the side chain. When a substituent is introduced at positions 4 or 5, the tautomeric character of the molecule precludes a definite numbering of these positions, resulting in names in the form "4(or 5)-substituted imidazole", as in |FRAME: CPD-54 "4(or 5)-aminoimidazole"|. However, when the imino hydrogen is substituted, tautomerism is no longer possible, and the numbering of positions 4 and 5 becomes absolute, as in |FRAME: CPD-19704|.

Compound.name: oxalate

Oxalate is toxic to mammals but is metabolized by many bacteria and plants by various pathways. In high concentrations, it causes death in humans and animals because of its corrosive effects, while smaller amounts can cause various pathological disorders, including hyperoxaluria, calcium oxalate stones, pyridoxine deficiency, and even renal failure. In oxalate-accumulating plants, calcium oxalate crystal accumulation occurs in specialized idioblast cells. The crystals are thought to deter herbivore feeding 16514014 and may also serve a role in regulating free calcium levels 15862089.

However, copper also binds tightly at the active sites of metalloenzymes, particularly those containing iron-sulfur clusters, resulting in destruction of their reactivity and the release of iron, which can produce reactive oxygen species (ROS). Thus, free copper ions rarely exist in cells |CITS: [10221913][12958362]|. Copper availability is largely constrained by the use of high-affinity sites in proteins 12738850. Copper homeostasis within cells include sensors, transporters, chaperones, and insertion proteins with high affinity and specificity for copper |CITS: [10816601][24205499][29414794]|.

The terphenylquinones are among the most prominent mushroom natural products. Their biosynthesis is elicited by cell wall damage caused by microbial lytic enzymes, suggesting a defensive role, which is supported by the fact that these compounds inhibit bacterial motility and modulate biofilms |CITS: [27699944][34081381]|. Atromentin was found to be a potent inhibitor of |FRAME: G-15302 FabK|, the enoyl-ACP reductase in |FRAME: TAX-1313| 17323650.

Despite that, many sera from tuberculous patients contain antibodies specifically recognizing the major PGL of the Canetti subspecies, |FRAME: CPD-18579|. The reason for the existence of the antibodies is that the strains that do not produce PGLs produce smaller molecules that contain a similar glycosylated aromatic moiety as that of |FRAME: CPD-18579|. Two such compounds have been described from |FRAME: TAX-83332|, which does not produce PGLs: |FRAME: CPD-18617|, which contains only one modifed rhamnosyl residue, and |FRAME: CPD-18619|, which contains the full tri-glycosylated moiety as PGL-tb 12138124. Since these compounds lack the long hydrocarbon chain found in PGLs, they are released into the culture medium instead of being attached to the hydrophobic mycobacterial cell surface. It is not known whether these compounds serve any purpose for the bacteria, or whether they are produced only as an artifact due to the mutation in the |FRAME: G-15015| gene encoding the PKS15/1 synthase, which prevents these bacteria from forming the phenolphthiocerol backbone 12138124.

Compound.name: spectinomycin
Synonyms: antibiotic 2233wp // espectinomicina // spectinomycin // spectinomycine // spectinomycinum // actinospectacin // trobicin
Comment: General Background |FRAME: CPD-22925 Spectinomycin| is an aminoglycoside antibiotic produced by |FRAME: TAX-68270| and related species. It has a unique tricyclic structure in which a single sugar component, |FRAME: CPD-27051|, is linked to the diaminocyclitol moiety (|FRAME: CPD-27044|) by beta-glycosidic and hemiketal bonds. |FRAME: CPD-22925 Spectinomycin| possesses a broad spectrum of activities against many Gram-positive as well as Gram-negative bacteria 4274968. It binds to the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, inhibiting the binding of the elongation factor G and interrupting protein synthesis. It possesses a particularly potent activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and is used (as its dihydrochloride pentahydrate) to treat gonorrhea in cases where the organism has acquired resistance to penicillin 14461632. Spectinomycin was discovered in 1961 under the name actinospectacin |CITS: [13767811][13711223][13761690][13867836]| and later sold under the trade name Trobicin (among others). It is included in the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.

The fully oxidized form, FAD, is converted to the reduced form, |FRAME: FADH2| by receiving two electrons and two protons. The reduced form can be oxidized to a |FRAME: FADH "semireduced form"| (semiquinone, FADH) by donating one electron and one proton. The semiquinone is then oxidized back to the fully oxidized form by losing a second electron and proton. Even though FAD has an aromatic ring system, FADH2 does not, making it significantly higher in energy. Many proteins contain a flavin moiety, either in the form of FAD or |FRAME: FMN|. They are known as |FRAME: Flavoproteins flavoproteins|.

The wound hormone is a compound that stimulates cell division near a trauma site to form a protective callus and to heal the damaged tissue. A quantitative assay for measuring the activity of the wound hormone was developed in 1927, measuring renewal of the parenchymous lining of the seed chambers of immature bean pods Wehnelt27. An active compound responsible for this activity was detected in 1937 and named traumatin for the Greek word trauma (wound) |CITS: [English37][17751236][16653492]|. However, two years later the authors reported that the compound is a dicarboxylic acid and renamed it accordingly as |FRAME: CPD-25932 "traumatic acid"| 17791417. With the discovery of |FRAME: 12-OXO-TRANS-10-DODECENOATE| in 1979 it was realized that the latter is the actual natural wound hormone, and that |FRAME: CPD-25932| is formed non-enzymatically by its oxidation in the presence of oxygen 16660762.

The most commonly found sources are |FRAME: TAX-33113| (the deadly nightshade), |FRAME: TAX-4075|, |FRAME: TAX-35625|, and |FRAME: TAX-4076|. Atropine is used as medication to treat certain types of nerve agent and pesticide poisonings, as well as some types of slow heart rate, and to decrease saliva production during surgery. It acts by being a competitive, reversible antagonist of the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor types M1, M2, M3, M4 and M5. Atropine is named after the belladonna plant |FRAME: TAX-33113|, from which a pure crystalline form was first prepared in 1833. However, atropine-containing extracts have been used for millenia. It ranks first on the priority list of Hazardous Substances published by the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR), based on a combination of frequency, toxicity, and potential for human exposure. It is also a Group 1 human carcinogen associated with skin, bladder and lung cancer. While arsenic exists in two oxidation states, As III and As V , in aerobic environments most inorganic arsenic is found as As(V), such as |FRAME: ARSENATE|. In anaerobic environments the prevalent form is As(III), such as |FRAME: CPD0-2040|. While most of the literature refers to the As(III) form found in the environment as |FRAME: CPD-763|, at natural pH values most of the As III molecules exist in solution as |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, an inorganic polyol similar to glycerol, since the pKa values are high: pKa 1 = 9:2 and pKa 2 = 12:7 |CITS: [11161507][15106984]|. This form of arsenite can enter cells via glycerol channels such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| or aquaglyceroporins, bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules such as glycerol to pass through. Charged forms of arsenite, formed at higher pH, include |FRAME: CPD-763 "arsenite 1- "|, |FRAME: CPD-24319| and |FRAME: CPD-24318|.

It has been suggested that this gas was responsible for an epidemic of sudden infant deaths that took place in Europe in the early 1830s, resulting from fumes produced by the molds growing on wallpapers decorated with arsenical colors such as |FRAME: CPD-24330| and |FRAME: CPD-24333|. While there has been accumulating suspicion that the source of the poisoning was the arsenical compounds 17745436, an exact mechanism of delivery was proposed by the Italian scientist Bartolomeo Gosio (1863-1944), who suggested that mold growing on the wallpaper converts the solid arsenical compounds into a volatile form. One of the mold strains identified by Gosio as responsilbe for this transformation is |FRAME: TAX-561152| |CITS: [17745435][Gosio93]|. Gosio incorrectly identified the main volatile product as |FRAME: CPD-24328| Gosio01. The true identity of the fungal volatile product as |FRAME: CPD-22659| was reported only in 1933 by the English chemist Frederick Challenger Challenger33, but |FRAME: CPD-22659| is still often referred to as Gosio gas 17733573. Ironically, |FRAME: CPD-22659| is actually not very toxic. Its LC 50 value is 20,000 ppm while that for |FRAME: CPD-24327| is only 0.05 ppm. It is now beleived that the gas was not the causative agent of the illness in the 19th century 15693178. A potential explanation may be the presence of the mold |FRAME: TAX-74722|, which produces airborne |FRAME: Mycotoxins mycotoxins| such as the |FRAME: Tricothecenes tricothecenes| |CITS: [11798344][15640178][16269780]|.

The |FRAME: Jasmonates jasmonates| are a group of important phytohormones, structurally similar to animal |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins| and ubiquitous in the plant kingdom. Many forms exist, based on the structure of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "Jasmonate"| (jasmonic acid, JA). The jasmonates act as regulatory molecules in many developmental processes that include fertility, sex determination, root elongation and fruit ripening. They are also potent signals activating plant defences against pathogens, herbivory, wounding and abiotic stress. The jasmonate regulation system includes the COI1 receptor protein and several JAZ ( JA smonate Z IM domain) repressors, which, in the absence of jasmonate, are bound to the MYC2 transcription factors, preventing transcription. In the presence of active jasmonate molecules, COI1 interacts with the JAZ repressors, causing their |FRAME: PWY-7511 ubiquitylation|. The ubiquitylated repressors are targeted for proteasome degradation, releasing the MYC2 transcription factors and activating transcription 19716757. Only two of the four stereoisomers of jasmonate occur naturally: |FRAME: CPD-731| and |FRAME: CPD-734| |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. These two forms are present in equilibrium within cells and can interconvert spontaneously through epimerization |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. The exact ratio of these stereoisomers within a cell has not been conclusively determined, and it may vary based on species, cell type, and physiological state. But, in the systems tested so far, |FRAME: CPD-734| is found at higher levels than |FRAME: CPD-731| 19349968. The biological activity of these stereoisomers can be quite different 8074303. Comment: |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes that facilitate the transfer of CO 2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation and transcarboxylation reactions involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [SHELLHAMMER90][11706201][15012185]|. The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX|, |FRAME: CPLX66-17|, |FRAME: CPLX-5203|, and |FRAME: CPLX-6001|) play essential roles in cell metabolism 8676868. Humans and other mammals cannot synthesize biotin and thus must obtain it from exogenous sources via intestinal absorption. Biotin was first discovered at the turn of the 20th century as a yeast growth factor, and was named bios Wildiers01. 30 years later, the compound was purified from egg yolk by Koegl and Toennis Koegl36. In a completely unrelated research, Gyoergy and his colleagues discovered biotin in liver in 1931, and isolated it in 1941. They named it vitamin H (for the German word for skin: Haut) Vigneaud41. At the same time, another group, which was working on Rhizobia bacteria, also identified it as an essential cofactor, which they named coenzyme R Allison38. Already in 1933, Gyoergy suggested that coenzyme R, bios and vitamin H were all the same molecule. The structure of biotin was solved in 1941 -1942 |CITS: [Vigneaud41B][Melville42]|. In 1949 the first evidence was published demonstrating the biochemical role of biotin in carboxylation reactions, Lardy49, and in 1958 it was suggested that biotin was probably associated with an enzyme 13560478. Shortly after this finding, Lynen et al Lynen61 described biotin's biological function as a cofactor in the biotin-dependent carboxylases. (This historical background is adapted from 12658511).

Peptidoglycan has been described as a fisherman's net. Comment: Bile (or gall) is a dark green to yellowish brown fluid, produced by the liver of most vertebrates, that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine. In humans bile is produced continuously by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. After eating, the bile is discharged into the the first section of the small intestine (the duodenum). The main active ingredient (about 0.7%) of the bile is bile acids. Bile acids are classified into primary and secondary. The primary bile acids are produced in the liver from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|. About half of the cholesterol produced in the body is used for bile acid synthesis. Their structures vary, as do their proportions in different species. The primary bile acids are conjugated in the liver with |FRAME: GLY| or |FRAME: TAURINE| before secretion into the bile. Further conversion into secondary bile acids occurs through the action of microbial enzymes in the gut. The primary bile acids |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189| are synthesized from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| by a series of oxidative transformations in the liver. They are further modified by attachemnt of a glycine or taurine molecule, forming |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, and |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see |FRAME: PWY-6061|). Following a meal, the bile acids are secreted into the small intestine, where they play an important role in digestion by acting as detergents. The majority (~97%) of the bile acids are reabsorbed in the ileum and return to the liver. The rest enter the large intestine, where they are modified by bacteria into secondary bile acids. The principal actions of gut bacteria on bile acids are C24-amide hydrolysis (releasing the glycine and taurine molecules) and 7alpha-dehydroxylation, forming |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| 26192599.

Comment: Cyclosporin A is a non-ribosomal cyclic peptide synthesized by the insect-pathogenic fungus |FRAME: TAX-29910|. The fungus was isolated in 1969 by Dr. H. P. Frey, an employee of Sandoz Pharmaceutical Corporation (now Novartis), from a soil sample taken during a vacation in Hardanger Vidda, Norway. Similar compounds were also identified in another fungus, |FRAME: TAX-301100|, which was collected at about the same time in Wisconsin, USA Borel95. It was named cyclosporin as it was a cyclical peptide derived from spores. Cyclosporine A was eventually found to selectively inhibit both the ability of the immune system to reject foreign tissues, as in transplantation, and chronic immune-mediated inflammation, as in autoimmunity. Since it is largely free of the life-threatening side-effects of previously-used immunosupressants, it revolutionized the field of transplantation. It is the active agent in the immunosuppressant drugs Sandimmune® and Neoral®, both manufactured by Sandoz. The cyclosporins were initially isolated as a mixture based on their antifungal activity, which was found to be quite low. However, their immunosupressant activity was discovered by Sandoz in 1971 |CITS: [Borel95][8575558][23331048]|. The two components of the mixture, |FRAME: CPD-20532| and |FRAME: CPD-26318|, were separated, and the structure of the main compound, |FRAME: CPD-20532|, was reported in 1976 |CITS: [950308][931750][893116]|. Many similar compounds were also identified, all of which cyclic peptides of 11 amino acids, seldom differing by more than two amino acids |CITS: [Dreyfuss76][3725752][3076967]|. Chemical synthesis was reported in 1986 |CITS: [3546034][3725755]|, resulting in the synthesis of thousands of semisynthetic or fully synthetic analogs. The cyclosporins are produced in a pathway that involves a 1.4 MDa non-ribosomal peptide synthase |CITS: [1820050][1637876][1644193][8300618]|. The biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-29910| was identified in 2013 23818858 and a biosynthetic pathway has been proposed 30279281.

Comment: |FRAME: MORPHINE "Morphine"| is an alkaloid found only in opium poppy (|FRAME: TAX-3469|) and related species (e.g., |FRAME: TAX-215229|). Opium alkaloids, including morphine, are known to act as chemical defense compounds to protect opium poppy against various herbivores. In response to stress, the capsules of opium poppies immediately metabolize morphine to dimeric morphine species, called |FRAME: CPD-12315| and |FRAME: CPD-12316|. These compounds bind to the cell wall polysaccharide pectins, resulting in cross-linking pectins to each other through bismorphine bridges and leading to resistance against hydrolysis by pectinase |CITS:[11498543][12880320]|. Morphine is an extremely potent opiate analgesic psychoactive drug in mammals, due to its strong binding to the opioid receptors, a group of G-protein coupled receptors. It is used extensively in medicine to relieve severe or agonizing pain and suffering.

Compound.name: sucrose
Comment: |FRAME: SUCROSE Sucrose| is the major product of photosynthesis in most plants and is known to be essential for their growth, development, carbon storage, signal transduction and stress protection 11005202. Sucrose is also found in cyanobacteria, and the ability to synthesize sucrose is a widespread feature of these organisms 21054739. In addition, sucrose is produced by many nonphotosynthetic aerobic methanotrophic and methanol-utilizing bacteria |CITS: [1055047][12656177][14529181][23808151][23865613]|. In photosynthetic organisms, the product of photosynthetic carbon fixation (|FRAME: GAP|) is transported from the chloroplast into the cytoplasm, where it is transformed to hexose phosphate by enzymes of the |FRAME: GLUCONEO-PWY gluconeogenesis| pathway. In plants, these hexose phosphates are used to synthesize sucrose, the form in which most fixed organic carbon is translocated from photosynthetic tissue to non-photosynthetic organs. Sucrose also provides substrates for plant storage glycosides such as |FRAME: Starch starch| and |FRAME: Fructans fructans|. Storage glycosides, including sucrose, are mobilized and utilized during seed germination and plant growth. In marine and freshwater cyanobacteria sucrose fulfils a different role. It is often synthesized in response to salt or temperature stress and seems to maintain the osmotic balance and to stabilize protein and membrane structure and function |CITS: [Reed86][7854254]|. Methanotrophic and methanol-utilizing bacteria also synthesize sucrose as a secondary osmotic compound, along with the major compatible solute |FRAME: ECTOINE| 25577257.

Compound.name: ergothioneine
Synonyms: N alpha , N alpha , N alpha -trimethyl-2-sulfanylidene-2,3-dihydro-L-histidine
Comment: |FRAME: Ergothioneine Ergothioneine| (EGT) is a histidine derivative with a thiol group attached to the C2 atom of the imidazole ring and a trimethylated amine. EGT was initially isolated in 1909 by Tanret from |FRAME: TAX-5111| (ergot), the fungal infection of rye grain Tanret09, and its structure was determined within two years Barger11. It has been reported only from certain fungi, actinomycetales bacteria and cyanobacteria |CITS: [13376573][13405916][Pfeiffer11]|. While the full function of EGT in the microbial cells is not well understood, it has been shown to play a pivotal role in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13893|, where it helps to activate an amine sugar before its condensation with an amino acid 25607359. EGT has also been proposed to protect cells from oxidative stress |CITS: [Garay56][2172707][22001064]|. The most significant difference between EGT and other biological thiols is the instability of the EGT disulfide under physiological conditions. Unlike other small thiols such as |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|, EGT is stable in its reduced form in aerated aqueous solutions and does not form the disulfide 15730267. Another significant difference is that EGT exists predominantly as the |FRAME: Ergothioneine-Thione "thione form"| at physiological pH 22001064. Although EGT is not synthesized by non-fungal eukaryotes, animals and plants acquire EGT from the environment through a specific transporter, ETT/OCTN1 15795384. It has been shown that the human body absorbs it from dietary sources and concentrates it in specific tissues or cells such as liver, kidney, central nervous system, and red blood cells 2172707. Both hyperactivity and deficiency of the OCTN1 transporter exert negative effects on human cells |CITS: [15795384][19136526]|. The precise function of ergothioneine in human tissue is also uncertain 17616140.

A second role is in the production of a modified tRNA nucleoside (|FRAME: 5-METHYLAMINOMETHYL-2-SELENOURIDINE|). A third role of Se, found in some bacteria, is in |FRAME: CPD-17760|, which serves as a cofactor for some hydroxylases. |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| is present in several enzymes, including |FRAME: CPLX-5881 "glutathione peroxidase"|, |FRAME: THYROXINE-DEIODINASE-RXN "thyroxine deiodinase"|, thioredoxin reductases, |FRAME: FORMATEDEHYDROGH-MONOMER|, |FRAME: CPLX-7378| and some hydrogenases. Compound.name: (3R)-linalool
Comment: |FRAME: Linalools Linalool| (3,7-dimethyl-1,6-octadien-3-ol) is an acyclic monoterpene alcohol with a pleasant fragrance associated with a diverse array of plants |CITS: [7522061][RAGUSO]|. It is found in lavender, bergamot, jasmine, basil, rosemary, sage, star-anise, cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, coriander, cardamom, ginger, black pepper and mandarin, and is one of the three terpene compounds principally responsible for Muscat aroma. Linalool is a primary compound in floral scent research. Both enantiomeric forms, |FRAME: CPD-8996| and |FRAME: CPD-8997|, occur in nature. Linalool is involved as an attractant in plant interactions with pollinators, herbivores and parasitoids RAGUSO. It has also been shown to be induced by artificial wounding and by jasmonic acid 17440821. The de novo synthesis of linalool has been demonstrated in floral tissues 17440821, barks and roots RAGUSO. Junipers, dicots and monocots emit linalool along with other monoterpenoids RAGUSO. Even though fungi typically do not produce monoterpenes, the de novo synthesis of linalool was demonstrate in some fungi, including the wine yeast strain, Saccharomyces cerevisiae M522, in the absence of grape derived precursors 15668008. |FRAME: CPD-8996| and its acetate ester are the only components of an essential oil produced by |FRAME: TAX-650269| (bergamot mint) 12176064. Other well-documented plants producing |FRAME: CPD-8996| include |FRAME: TAX-39329| (lavender) 17662687, the traditional Chinese medical herb |FRAME: TAX-35608| 10562427, and |FRAME: TAX-4081| (tomato) 17440821.

Compound.name: pppGpp
Comment: The nucleotides |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-diphosphate) and |FRAME: GDP-TP| (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-triphosphate), referred to collectively as (p)ppGpp, have been shown to regulate gene expression during the stringent response in some bacteria. Their levels become elevated during this response and they are key indicators and regulators of it. The stringent response is a global regulatory system that operates under conditions of nutrient or energy starvation or other environmental stress. It has varying effects on gene expression and metabolism. In addition to bacteria, there is evidence that (p)ppGpp may regulate transcription by plastid-encoded RNA polymerase in plant chloroplasts 19308923. Due to its role as an effector molecule in the stringent response in bacteria, (p)ppGpp has been described as a bacterial alarmone. It can contribute to the regulation of various cellular processes that are affected by nutritional stress such as growth, cell division, motility, adaptation and virulence. Its effect on the pathogenicity of some bacteria has led to the development of ppGpp analogs as possible antibacterial compounds 18776539 and new in vitro synthesis 18789883 and detection 18166051 methods for ppGpp. Different bacteria have different ways of synthesizing and responding to (p)ppGpp, many of which are still being discovered. Even in the well-studied TAX-562 many details of ppGpp action remain to be elucidated. Reviewed in |CITS: [18454629] [15866041] [18359660]|.

Comment: Bilirubin is a yellow compound that is produced in vertebrates during heme degradation and is excreted in bile and urine. During the degradation the porphyrin ring of heme is broken, so bilirubin consists of an open chain of four pyrrole-like rings. Several enzymes that cleave the heme ring exist, cleaving it at different positions and generating different bilirubin compounds. The most common enzyme, which is also found in mammals, produces |FRAME: BILIRUBIN|. The structure of bilirubin-IX alpha was originally established by Hans Fischer in 1941, who did not specify the isomeric configuration Fischer41. It was later shown that the naturally occurring form of bilirubin is the |FRAME: BILIRUBIN " Z,Z isomer"| Lemberg49. However, when exposed to light, the Z,Z isomer converts to an |FRAME: CPD-20930 E,E isomer"|. Unconjugated bilirubin is extremely water insoluble. It is carried (mostly by albumin) to the liver, where it is converted to glucuronides, which are water soluble. The glucuronides are eventually excreted in bile. Glucuronated forms include both monoglucuronides (a mixture of the two positional isomers |FRAME: CPD-20932| and |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-GLUCURONOSIDE|) and |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-BISGLUCURONOSIDE| |CITS: [5145912][949313][7378044]|. Four basic forms of bilirubin are found in blood: |FRAME: BILIRUBIN "unconjugated bilirubin"| (alpha bilirubin), |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-GLUCURONOSIDE "mono-conjugated"| (beta bilirubin), |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-BISGLUCURONOSIDE "di-conjugated"| (gamma bilirubin), and protein bound (delta bilirubin) 5902889.

Compound.name: thiamine
Comment: Thiamin(e), also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the polishing of rice, the main staple, resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk Begley96. The anti-beriberi substance was crystallized from rice polishings by Jansen and Donath in 1926 Jansen26. The structure and synthesis of thiamine were reported by Williams Williams38. The compound was named thiamine because it was believed to be an amine. When it became clear that it is not an amine, it was proposed to drop the 'e' and use simply thiamin 16550223. Today both names are used, but thiamine is more prevalent.

Compound.name: isoprene
Comment: Isoprene is a volatile compound produced by many plants. The yearly production of isoprene emissions by vegetation is around 600 million tonnes (with half of it coming from tropical broadleaf trees), making it about a third of all hydrocarbons released into the atmosphere Guenther06. Isoprene is incorporated into cell membranes in response to heat stress, and its stabilizing effect confers some tolerance to heat spikes. Its emission increases dramatically with temperature and maximizes at around 40 °C. Thus, it is thought that isoprene protects plants against heat stress 17921528. It also confers some resistance to reactive oxygen species 19183288. Isoprene is a common structural motif in biological polymers, although those compounds (|FRAME: Polyisoprenoids isoprenoids|) are not derived from isoprene, but instead are synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-4211| and its isomer |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|. Isoprene is used to produce a diverse range of industrial products including a wide variety of specialty elastomers used in surgical gloves, motor mounts and fittings, rubber bands, golf balls, and shoes. It is also used as a component of Styrene-isoprene-styrene block copolymers that form an essential part of most hot-melt pressure-sensitive adhesive formulations, and of cis -polyisoprene or synthetic rubber, which is used in tire manufacturing Whited2010.

Binding of endocannabinoids (or cannabinoids) to cannabinoid receptors results in a decrease in the intracellular level of |FRAME: CAMP| and activation of |FRAME: EC-2.7.11.24|, through the coupled Gi/o proteins. In addition, the activation of cannabinoid receptors modulates ion channels through Gi/o proteins, leading to the activation of A-type and inward-rectifyier potassium channels and the inhibition of N-type and P/Q-type calcium channels 19126434. |FRAME: CPD-7598 "Anandamide"| is synthesized from |FRAME: N-arachidonoyl-PE " N -arachidonoyl phosphatidylethanolamine"| by multiple pathways 19126434. Comment: This is a naturally occurring form of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "jasmonic acid"| |CITS:[8074303][19349968]| in plants. The |FRAME: Jasmonates jasmonates| are a group of important phytohormones, structurally similar to animal |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins| and ubiquitous in the plant kingdom. Many forms exist, based on the structure of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "Jasmonate"| (jasmonic acid, JA). The jasmonates act as regulatory molecules in many developmental processes that include fertility, sex determination, root elongation and fruit ripening. They are also potent signals activating plant defences against pathogens, herbivory, wounding and abiotic stress. The jasmonate regulation system includes the COI1 receptor protein and several JAZ ( JA smonate Z IM domain) repressors, which, in the absence of jasmonate, are bound to the MYC2 transcription factors, preventing transcription. In the presence of active jasmonate molecules, COI1 interacts with the JAZ repressors, causing their |FRAME: PWY-7511 ubiquitylation|. The ubiquitylated repressors are targeted for proteasome degradation, releasing the MYC2 transcription factors and activating transcription 19716757. Only two of the four stereoisomers of jasmonate occur naturally: |FRAME: CPD-731| and |FRAME: CPD-734| |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. These two forms are present in equilibrium within cells and can interconvert spontaneously through epimerization |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. The exact ratio of these stereoisomers within a cell has not been conclusively determined, and it may vary based on species, cell type, and physiological state. But, in the systems tested so far, |FRAME: CPD-734| is found at higher levels than |FRAME: CPD-731| 19349968. The biological activity of these stereoisomers can be quite different 8074303. In addition, enzymes involved in JA metabolism may have different preferences for the different stereoisomers 17291501.

Nicotinate is one of three forms of vitamin B 3 : |FRAME: NIACINE|, |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE|, and |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_RIBOSE "nicotinamide riboside"| [more accurately named 1-(beta-D ribofuranosyl)nicotinamide]. These three forms are interchangeable, and are usually used for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: NAD| |CITS: [Elvehjem38][15137942]|. |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_RIBOSE| can be converted to |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| by |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.3| |FRAME: RXN-8441| and |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| can be hydrolyzed to |FRAME: NIACINE| by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.19| (which is not present in humans) |FRAME: NICOTINAMID-RXN| Eukaryotes and prokaryotes produce NAD de novo from |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, respectively, by pathways that bypasses vitamin B3 compounds and instead proceed via |FRAME: NICOTINATE_NUCLEOTIDE| (see |FRAME: NADSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|). Vitamin B3 compounds are used in NAD salvage pathways such as |FRAME: PWY-5381| and |FRAME: PWY3O-4106| |CITS: [13563526][13563527][15137942]|. In populations with a tryptophan-poor diet the NAD de novo biosynthesis pathway is not sufficient to produce the required NAD, making the salvage pathways that rely on vitamin B 3 compounds the main source of NAD. It is produced as an active metabolic product of testosterone. In premenapausal women 17beta-estradiol is produced by the granulosa cells of the ovaries by the aromatization of |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| (via |FRAME: ESTRONE|). The same occurs in men in the testes. Compound.name: NAD +
Synonyms: NAD+ // beta-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide // coenzyme I // diphosphopyridine nucleotide // diphosphopyridine nucleotide oxidized // nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide // nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide oxidized // NAD-oxidized // NAD-ox // DPN+ // DPN-ox // DPN // beta-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide // NAD // beta-NAD +
Comment: |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as |FRAME: Cofactors cofactors|. They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes". The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form. |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|).

Compound.name: ppGpp
Synonyms: guanosine tetraphosphate // guanosine 5'-diphosphate,3'-diphosphate // guanosine 3',5'-bispyrophosphate // guanosine 3',5'-bis(diphosphate) // guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-diphosphate // magic spot // guanosine-5',3'-tetraphosphate
Comment: The nucleotides |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-diphosphate) and |FRAME: GDP-TP| (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-triphosphate), referred to collectively as (p)ppGpp, have been shown to regulate gene expression during the stringent response in some bacteria. Their levels become elevated during this response and they are key indicators and regulators of it. The stringent response is a global regulatory system that operates under conditions of nutrient or energy starvation or other environmental stress. It has varying effects on gene expression and metabolism. In addition to bacteria, there is evidence that (p)ppGpp may regulate transcription by plastid-encoded RNA polymerase in plant chloroplasts 19308923. Due to its role as an effector molecule in the stringent response in bacteria, (p)ppGpp has been described as a bacterial alarmone. It can contribute to the regulation of various cellular processes that are affected by nutritional stress such as growth, cell division, motility, adaptation and virulence. Its effect on the pathogenicity of some bacteria has led to the development of ppGpp analogs as possible antibacterial compounds 18776539 and new in vitro synthesis 18789883 and detection 18166051 methods for ppGpp. Different bacteria have different ways of synthesizing and responding to (p)ppGpp, many of which are still being discovered. Even in the well-studied TAX-562 many details of ppGpp action remain to be elucidated. Reviewed in |CITS: [18454629] [15866041] [18359660]|.

The indolmycin structure contains an oxazolinone ring in its core, making it of interest to synthetic chemists, and over the years several total synthetic routes have been reported |CITS: [5729561][Takeda80][Dirlam86][Akita90][Witty96][Shue96][11767081][Sutou08]|. Comment: |FRAME: GLT| is one of the proteinogenic amino acids. It is named after wheat gluten, from which it was described in 1866 by the German chemist Karl Heinrich Ritthausen. |FRAME: GLT| plays an important role in nitrogen metabolism in the cell. Once cells take up ammonium, it is fixed by incorporation into the TCA cycle intermediate |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.4|, forming |FRAME: GLT| 13239305 (an additional ammonium molecule can be fixed into L-glutamate, e.g. by |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.2|, forming |FRAME: GLN| 14833423). Glutamate then becomes the central source for passing amino groups on to other molecules by the action of transaminase (=aminotransferase) enzymes, distributing nitrogen throughout the cell. For example, glutamate can transfer the amino group to the common metabolites |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, forming |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, respectively. It has been estimated that glutamate and glutamine provide 75% and 25%, respectively, of all cellular nitrogen 30026566. In addition to its protein building role, |FRAME: GLT| is the most abundant excitatory neurotransmitter in the vertebrate nervous system, acting on ionotropic and metabotropic (G-protein coupled) receptors 10736372. |FRAME: GLT| interacts with the umami taste receptors, which sense glutamates and nucleotides, imparting "meaty", "savory", and "broth-like" flavor. The monosodium salt of glutamate (MSG), which is found naturally in some foods, is often added to foodstuff for flavoring 1679557. Although MSG is commnly believed to cause headaches, all scientific studies found no such effect 27189588.

Compound.name: plastoquinol-9
Comment: |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE Plastoquinones| (PQ) are benzoquinone electron carriers that can function as acceptor/donor for either one or two electrons. They are analogs of |FRAME: Ubiquinones "ubiquinones"| (Coenzyme Q), with two methyl groups substituting the methoxy groups found in Q. The fully reduced form is called |FRAME: Plastoquinols|. Plastoquinones are found in the chloroplasts of higher plants, red, brown and green algae, and in cyanobacteria, and are important members of the photosynthetic electron transfer chain, where they carry electrons from |FRAME: CPLX490-3506| to the |FRAME: CPLX-9022|. In fact, it has been shown that in cyanobacteria essentially all electron transport through unbound quinones proceeds via PQ in cyanobacterial thylakoids. Apart from PQ the only quinone found in thylakoids is vitamin K1, which is associated with PS I Vermaas01. Plastoquinones also serve as cofactors involved in the desaturation of phytoene in the synthesis of carotenoids (see |FRAME: PWY-6475|). Plastoquinone was isolated originally in 1946 from alfalfa, but was not identified at the time. It was rediscovered in 1959 and its structure described in the same year (see 7022156).

It includes several compounds often referred to as vitamin B12, that differ in the upper axial ligand. The functional forms of the B12 vitamin, CPD-9037 and ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN, include either a methyl group or an 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as their upper axial ligand, respectively. Other forms of cobalamin include |FRAME: CPD0-1256| (or its conjugated acid |FRAME: AQUACOBIIIALAMIN|) and |FRAME: CPD-315|. |FRAME: CPD0-1256 Hydroxocobalamin| is a naturally produced form synthesized by many bacterial species, while |FRAME: CPD-315| is a common semi-synthetic form produced from bacterially-synthesized |FRAME: CPD0-1256|. Vitamin B12 pills often contain |FRAME: CPD-315|, which is converted to the active forms in the body. The cobalt ion embedded in cobalamin may exist in different oxidation states (+1, +2 or +3), and the different forms of the compound are referred to as |FRAME: COB-I-ALAMIN|, |FRAME: CPD-1829| and |FRAME: CPD-17105|, respectively.

Carnitine was first discovered in 1905 in muscle extracts, and the name is derived from the Latin word for flesh, Carnis 11183736. In 1962 it was found that the physiological enantiomer is |FRAME: CARNITINE|, and since then the widespread distribution of L-carnitine has been established in higher and lower eukaryotes, plants, and many microorganisms 9706218. In animals and yeast carnitine is best known for its contribution to fatty acid intracellular trafficking 2199593. In plants L-carnitine is also associated with fatty acid metabolism, although its exact function is less well understood |CITS: [17988884][30080631]|. Bacteria are not able to synthesize carnitine do novo , but are able to import the compound and use it as an osmoprotectant or to enhance thermotolerance, cryotolerance and barotolerance 25787873. |FRAME: CARNITINE| is used in pharmaceutical and nutritional preparations and methods have been described for its production and separation from its |FRAME: D-CARNITINE| enantiomer |CITS: [12191705 ] [9830124]| and reviewed in 17910757.

Compound.name: urea
Comment: Urea is the main nitrogen-containing substance in the urine of most land animals, with the exception of birds and saurian reptiles, which excrete |FRAME: URATE "uric acid"|. It was discovered in 1773 by Hilaire Rouelle who isolated it from human urine. The |FRAME: UREA| is often formed by a cyclic pathway known as the urea cycle. In this cycle, amino groups donated by AMMONIA and L-ASPARTATE are converted to UREA, while L-ORNITHINE, L-CITRULLINE, L-ARGININO-SUCCINATE, and ARG act as intermediates. Urea was first synthesized from inorganic compounds in 1828 by Friedrich Wohler, being the first organic compound to be synthesized from inorganic materials. Today more than 90% of the world industrial production of urea is destined for use as a nitrogen-release fertilizer.

Compound.name: ( Z,Z )-bilirubin-IX alpha
Comment: Bilirubin is a yellow compound that is produced in vertebrates during heme degradation and is excreted in bile and urine. During the degradation the porphyrin ring of heme is broken, so bilirubin consists of an open chain of four pyrrole-like rings. Several enzymes that cleave the heme ring exist, cleaving it at different positions and generating different bilirubin compounds. The most common enzyme, which is also found in mammals, produces |FRAME: BILIRUBIN|. The structure of bilirubin-IX alpha was originally established by Hans Fischer in 1941, who did not specify the isomeric configuration Fischer41. It was later shown that the naturally occurring form of bilirubin is the |FRAME: BILIRUBIN " Z,Z isomer"| Lemberg49. However, when exposed to light, the Z,Z isomer converts to an |FRAME: CPD-20930 E,E isomer"|. Unconjugated bilirubin is extremely water insoluble. It is carried (mostly by albumin) to the liver, where it is converted to glucuronides, which are water soluble. The glucuronides are eventually excreted in bile. Glucuronated forms include both monoglucuronides (a mixture of the two positional isomers |FRAME: CPD-20932| and |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-GLUCURONOSIDE|) and |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-BISGLUCURONOSIDE| |CITS: [5145912][949313][7378044]|. Four basic forms of bilirubin are found in blood: |FRAME: BILIRUBIN "unconjugated bilirubin"| (alpha bilirubin), |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-GLUCURONOSIDE "mono-conjugated"| (beta bilirubin), |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-BISGLUCURONOSIDE "di-conjugated"| (gamma bilirubin), and protein bound (delta bilirubin) 5902889.

The main functions of taurine in mammals include bile acid conjugation, detoxification, osmoregulation, membrane stabilization, and regulation of intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis.

Compound.name: chlorophyll c 2
Comment: |FRAME: Chlorophylls Chlorophyll| is a green photosynthetic pigment found in photosynthetic plants, algae, and bacteria. Its name is derived from ancient Greek: chloros = green and phyllon = leaf. Chlorophyll functions as the main light harvesting pigment in photosynthesis, capturing photons and transfering them to the reaction centers. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly in the blue and, to a lesser extent, red portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, hence its intense green color. There are several variants of chlorophyll (|FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, |FRAME: CPD-10334|, |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|, |FRAME: CPD-18895|, |FRAME: CPD-10336|, |FRAME: CPD-10337|, |FRAME: CPD-10335|, |FRAME: CPD-18896|, |FRAME: CPD-18897| and |FRAME: CPD-18898|). Chlorophyll c is found in certain marine algae, including the photosynthetic Chromista (e.g. diatoms, brown algae) and dinoflagellates. It acts as an accessory pigment, particularly significant in its absorption of light in the 447-452 nm region 5439971. |FRAME: CPD-10337 "Chlorophyll c 2 "| is the most common form of chlorophyll c . Chlorophyll c is unusual because it has a porphyrin ring structure and does not have an isoprenoid tail or a reduced D ring like other types of chlorophyll. |FRAME: CPD-10336 "Chlorophyll c 1 "| has an ethyl group at carbon C8, while |FRAME: CPD-10337| has a C8 vinyl group 16667093.

Phthiocerols comprise a linear carbohydrate molecule to which one methoxyl group, one methyl group, and two secondary hydroxyl groups are attached. Two types of phthiocerols have been described. In |FRAME: Phthiocerol-A "phthiocerol A"| the methoxyl and methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: TAX-1781| and |FRAME: TAX-1809|, however, they are esterified by |FRAME: Phthioceranic-Acids "phthioceranic acids"| |CITS: [3149973][3113946]|.

(+)-Nootkatone also possess neuroprotective effects |CITS: [29177693][31422511]| and may be a potential therapeutic treatment for neuroinflammation and Alzheimer's disease |CITS: [29990697][31542420]|.

It has also been shown to be induced by artificial wounding and by jasmonic acid 17440821. The de novo synthesis of linalool has been demonstrated in floral tissues 17440821, barks and roots RAGUSO. Junipers, dicots and monocots emit linalool along with other monoterpenoids RAGUSO. Compound.name: cholate
Comment: Bile (or gall) is a dark green to yellowish brown fluid, produced by the liver of most vertebrates, that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine. In humans bile is produced continuously by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. After eating, the bile is discharged into the the first section of the small intestine (the duodenum). The main active ingredient (about 0.7%) of the bile is bile acids. Bile acids are classified into primary and secondary. The primary bile acids are produced in the liver from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|. About half of the cholesterol produced in the body is used for bile acid synthesis. Their structures vary, as do their proportions in different species. The primary bile acids are conjugated in the liver with |FRAME: GLY| or |FRAME: TAURINE| before secretion into the bile. Further conversion into secondary bile acids occurs through the action of microbial enzymes in the gut. The primary bile acids |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189| are synthesized from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| by a series of oxidative transformations in the liver. They are further modified by attachemnt of a glycine or taurine molecule, forming |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, and |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see |FRAME: PWY-6061|). Following a meal, the bile acids are secreted into the small intestine, where they play an important role in digestion by acting as detergents. The majority (~97%) of the bile acids are reabsorbed in the ileum and return to the liver. The rest enter the large intestine, where they are modified by bacteria into secondary bile acids. The principal actions of gut bacteria on bile acids are C24-amide hydrolysis (releasing the glycine and taurine molecules) and 7alpha-dehydroxylation, forming |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| 26192599.

Synonyms: H4PteGlu // 5,6,7,8-tetrahydrofolic acid // tetrahydrofolic acid // (6S)-tetrahydrofolate // H 4 PteGlu 1 // tetrahydrofolate // tetrahydrafolate // tetrahydropteroyl mono-L-glutamate // THF // tetra-H-folate // th-folate // FH4 // folate-H4 // tetrahydropteroylglutamate // H4F // vitamin B9
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551.

Comment: The genus |FRAME: TAX-26496| is the most important genus of the |FRAME: TAX-26468| family, which comprises approximately 190 species of trees and lianas. |FRAME: CPD-21554 Strychnine| is a terpene indole alkaloid belonging to the Strychnos family of Corynanthe alkaloids and was the first alkaloid to be identified in plants of the |FRAME: TAX-26496| genus. It is found in the seeds and bark of many plants in this genus. |FRAME: TAX-28545| is a tree native to the tropical forests on the Malabar Coast in Southern India, Sri Lanka and Indonesia. It has an orange-colored fruit that contains five seeds. The toxic effects of these seeds have been well known from the times of ancient India, although the chemical compound itself was not identified. In 1819, Pelletier and Caventou reported the isolation of strychnine, in pure form, as the principal toxin from |FRAME: TAX-28545| and |FRAME: TAX-1037790| Pelletier19. The correct structure was reported in 1946 |CITS: [Briggs46][Holmes46]|. The absolute stereochemistry of strychnine was established by Peerdeman in 1956 with X-ray crystallographic analysis Peerdeman56. Strychnine is one of the most complex natural products of its size, with twenty-four skeletal atoms arranged in seven rings, resulting in six contiguous stereogenic centers. Strychnine is a powerful toxin (a lethal dose of strychnine for an adult human is in the range of 30-100 mg). It is an antagonist of glycine and acetylcholine receptors and affects primarily the motor nerve fibers in the spinal cord which control muscle contraction. It binds noncovalently to the same receptor as glycine, preventing the inhibitory effects of glycine on the postsynaptic neuron and resulting in activation of the motor neurons. This activation causes spastic muscle contractions and eventually death by asphyxiation.

It features an unusual 1,3-dioxo-1,2-dithiolane moiety that is spiro-fused to a thiazole-containing 18-membered lactam ring, a molecular architecture that hasn't been found in any other natural product. LNM possesses potent DNA cleavage activity via an unprecedented mode of action. Upon the attack of cellular thiol agents at the 1,3-dioxo-1,2-dithiolane moiety, the compound undergoes a tandem rearrangement to form an episulfonium ion intermediate that can efficiently alkylate the N-7 position of deoxyguanosine bases of DNA |CITS: [11080040][21954957][22682923][26071634][29231931]|. This unique mode of action confers potent cytotoxicity against tumors including those resistant to clinically important anticancer drugs, making LNM a promising anticancer drug lead. Total synthesis of LNM has been accomplished Kanda93, followed by assorted chemical modifications |CITS: [9871510][10212117][Kanda03]| and generation of functional mimics |CITS: [8639657][12708847]|.

Comment: Thiols play a major role in the detoxification of stress-inducing factors such as reactive oxygen species, free radicals, peroxides, lipid peroxides, and heavy metals. In mammals, the major thiol is the tripeptide |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| (gamma-Glu-Cys-Gly, known as GSH). Toxins are conjugated to GSH in the liver by a dedicated enzyme, resulting in a |FRAME: S-Substituted-L-Cysteines "cysteine-toxin conjugate"|. The conjugate is acetylated in the kidney to form |FRAME: Mercapturates|, and is then excreted 8145281 (see |FRAME: PWY-4061|). In addition to oxidative stress management, low molecular weight thiols have been found to be involved in critical cellular processes including DNA synthesis and formaldehyde reduction Patel98. Gluathione is the major thiol not only in eukaryotic organisms but also in Gram negative bacteria and in the majority of Gram positive bacteria. Pathogenic bacteria live in a particularly hostile environment, in which the host deliberately generates toxins, including reactive oxygen species, to destroy the invading organism, thus thiols are particularly important for the survival of these organisms. Despite the ubiquity of GSH, it is not universal. In many organisms, including some eukaryotes, other thiols have taken its role. Some of these thiols are |FRAME: CoM|, |FRAME: TRYPANOTHIONE|, |FRAME: Ergothioneine|, |FRAME: CPD1G-2| and |FRAME: CPD-17028|.

Compound.name: scyllo -inositol
Comment: |FRAME: Inositols Inositol| is the generic name for 1,2,3,4,5,6-cyclohexanehexol. Epimerization of the six hydroxyl groups results in nine stereoisomers. Among the isomers, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| is the most abundant in nature and it is an essential compound in eukaryotic cell membranes as a phosphatidylinositol moiety, which plays an important role in signal transduction. Some other forms, such as |FRAME: CPD-8050|, are also found in nature, although they are less abundant. Nomenclature of cyclitols can be quite confusing. Two alternative naming schemes are possible for inositol compounds since carbon-1 could be assigned to either of two enantiotopic carbons. The two methods result in 1D-stereochemistry and 1L-stereochemistry based names. If carbon-1 is placed at the top of the molecule, L-numbering proceeds clockwise, while D-numbering proceeds counter-clockwise. Both the 1D or 1L designations can be employed currently. However, the symbol Ins implies myo-inositol with D- numbering. Additional information on the nomenclature of myo -inositol compounds can be found in the 1973 document Nomenclature of cyclitols by the Nomenclature Committee of the International Union of Biochemistry (NC-IUB), and the 1988 publication Numbering of atoms in myo -inositol , published by the same body, whose aim was to relax some of the rules specified in the 1973 publication. To aid in following the transformations in inositol compounds in pathways, the structures of inositol stereoisomers in MetaCyc have been formatted to show carbon 1 at the top of the ring, with numbering proceeding clockwise. An exception is the structure of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, which is presented with carbon 3 at the top and counter-clockwise numbering. The reason is that carbon 3 of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| (which is based on L-numbering) matches the carbon-1 of 1D numbering, which is used for the various phosphorylated and otherwise modified forms, and by presenting the molecule in this way, it is much easier to show structural relationships in reactions and pathways (see for example |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL-1-KINASE-RXN "EC 2.7.1.64"|). |FRAME: CPD-8050 " Scyllo -inositol"| is a relatively rare form of |FRAME: Inositols inositol| but is sometimes found in organisms. It has been documented in |FRAME: TAX-13422| buds 10830508 and in |FRAME: TAX-4513 barley| seeds, where it is present in phosphatidylinositol 7755633. The phosphatidylinositol synthase of |FRAME: TAX-5919| can act on |FRAME: CPD-8050| 17403152. In mammals, |FRAME: CPD-8050| has been shown to localize in the kidney and brain 5644141, and an enzyme from bovine brain was found to interconvert |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| and |FRAME: CPD-8050| 1267771.

Comment: |FRAME: CPD-19894 Vincristine| is a bisindole alkaloid produced by the plant |FRAME: TAX-4058| (Madagascar periwinkle). The anti-proliferative properties of |FRAME: CPD-19894| were discovered by serendipity. A tea made from |FRAME: TAX-4058| has been used for a long time as a folk-remedy for diabetes. When the tea was tested in a lab in 1949, it failed to show any effect on diabetes. However, when the extract was injected into rats, they died within a few days from a bacterial infection. Further research has found that administering the extract by injection resulted in a severely reduced white blood cell count and bone marrow depression. An effort to identify the active compound started in 1955, and partially enriched material was shown to possess carcinostatic activity against transplantable mammary adenocarcinoma 13627916. The first compound to be purified was |FRAME: CPD-7858|, originally named vincaleukoblastine |CITS: [Noble58][13719013][13842983][14407465]|. However, studies have shown that the plant contains more than 70 different alkaloids, and |FRAME: CPD-19894| was isolated by 1963 14070392. Vincristine was approved as an anticancer drug by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in July 1963. The production of |FRAME: CPD-19894| from the |FRAME: TAX-4058| plant is very inefficient, resulting in very high prices. Initially one ton of dried leaves were used to produce one ounce of the pure compound 1489402.

Compound.name: ursodeoxycholate
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-10534 Ursodeoxycholate| (UDCA) is a bile acid that makes up a small percentage (< 5%) of the biliary pool in most healthy mammals. In most mammals it is a secondary bile acid, produced from primary bile acids by the action of intestinal bacteria. It is an important ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine, and has verified therapeutic benefits for the treatment of several ailments including cholestatic liver disease |CITS: [74722][7372061][7051912][16530513][17185355]| and colon cancer |CITS: [7923119][12839936][14747693]|. The name is derived from the Latin "ursus", which means bear, because it was originally discovered from the bile of the Polar bear (under the name ursocholeinsaure) |CITS: [Hammarsten01][Hammarsten02]|. Twenty-five years later, the compound was crystallized from a commercial preparation of bile of the Black bear, found to be an isomer of |FRAME: CPD-15189|, and named ursodeoxycholic acid Shoda27. Bears and the nutria (|FRAME: TAX-10157|) are the only mammals in which UDCA is a dominant primary biliary bile acid, being formed by hepatic enzymes |CITS: [Tammar70][Haslewood78][Hagey92]|. In all other species it appears to be a secondary bile acid, produced by bacteria from primary bile acids 8263415. Even though UDCA is chemically synthesized by multiple companies, several countries in East Asia, including China, South Korea, Laos, Vietnam, and Myanmar, still use "bile bears" - bears that are kept in captivity and used for harvesting their bile by surgery. Bear farming is extremely inhumane and many bears die of illness such as chronic infections and liver cancer. Despite being illegal in some of these countries, bear bile farming still exists in all of those countries and is a significant problem |CITS: [15066772][19138420]|. UDCA can be 7beta-dehydroxylated to |FRAME: CPD-7235| 7057103 or epimerized to |FRAME: CPD-15189| 6946176, which is then 7alpha-dehydroxylated to |FRAME: CPD-7235| as described in |FRAME: PWY-7754|.

Marine phytoplankton synthesize DMSP not only as an osmolyte, but also as a predator deterrent and an antioxidant 17068264. The degradation of DMSP to DMS and subsequent exchange of DMS across the ocean-atmosphere boundary is the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere.

Compound.name: dimethyl sulfide
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-7670 Dimethylsulfide| (DMS) is a major contributor to the total sulfur emissions to the atmosphere from land and the ocean. In marine, estuarine, and salt marsh systems, the main source of DMS is the degradation of |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN| (DMSP), an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants 15181109. DMSP is readily degraded in a variety of biological systems, including bacterial cultures, salt marsh sediments, and seawater samples containing algae and zooplankton 16347732. There are two main routes for DMSP degradation, leading to formation of either |FRAME: CPD-7670| or |FRAME: CPD-7672|. Other sources for DMS include the reduction of |FRAME: DMSO|, the methylation of |FRAME: CPD-7671|, and the degradation of sulfur-containing amino acids. DMS, which is very volatile, is exchanged freely between the ocean and the atmosphere, and is considered the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere. Once in the troposphere, DMS is oxidized to |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: CPD-3746|, which attract water and promote cloud formation and thus influence the climate Charlson87. However, up to 90% of the DMS in the ocean is degraded biologically Kiene90. DMS is toxic, and attempts to isolate in pure culture DMS-degrading organisms that can use it as the sole carbon and energy source have been often unsuccessful due to this toxicity. However, several organisms capable of degerading DMS have been isolated over the years. Aerobic bacterial DMS oxidation has been demonstrated in organisms from a few taxonomic domains, including Thiobacillus sp. strain MS1 Sivela80, |FRAME: ORG-5989| |CITS: [Kanagawa82] [Kanagawa86][2930168][Tanji89][Gould92]|, |FRAME: ORG-6053| |CITS: [1872604][8285684]|, |FRAME: ORG-6050| Debont81, |FRAME: ORG-6052| |CITS:[3767349][Suylen86][Suylen87][Smith88a]| and TAX-392484 |CITS:[16535680][17322322]|. Anaerobic degradation of DMS has been documented by methanogens 11073950 (see |FRAME: PWY-5258|) and by sulfate-reducing bacteria 8074524.

Comment: |FRAME: Chlorophylls Chlorophyll| is a green photosynthetic pigment found in photosynthetic plants, algae, and bacteria. Its name is derived from ancient Greek: chloros = green and phyllon = leaf. Chlorophyll functions as the main light harvesting pigment in photosynthesis, capturing photons and transfering them to the reaction centers. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly in the blue and, to a lesser extent, red portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, hence its intense green color. There are several variants of chlorophyll (|FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, |FRAME: CPD-10334|, |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|, |FRAME: CPD-18895|, |FRAME: CPD-10336|, |FRAME: CPD-10337|, |FRAME: CPD-10335|, |FRAME: CPD-18896|, |FRAME: CPD-18897| and |FRAME: CPD-18898|). Chlorophyll c is found in certain marine algae, including the photosynthetic Chromista (e.g. diatoms, brown algae) and dinoflagellates. It acts as an accessory pigment, particularly significant in its absorption of light in the 447-452 nm region 5439971. |FRAME: CPD-10337 "Chlorophyll c 2 "| is the most common form of chlorophyll c . Chlorophyll c is unusual because it has a porphyrin ring structure and does not have an isoprenoid tail or a reduced D ring like other types of chlorophyll. |FRAME: CPD-10336 "Chlorophyll c 1 "| has an ethyl group at carbon C8, while |FRAME: CPD-10337| has a C8 vinyl group 16667093.

Compound.name: formate
Comment: Formate is a one-carbon molecule that was first isolated from distillation of ant bodies, and it was subsequently named using the Latin word for ant, formica Stumper21. Ants and other insects accumulate formate in secretory glands and release their content as a mechanism of defense. Formate serves as an intermediate in one-carbon (1C) metabolism in all organisms. It is also a key metabolite for many bacterial and archaeal species. Depending on the physiological conditions, formate serves various roles, such as to act as a reductant in anaerobic respiration, be oxidized aerobically, be secreted, or be converted to hydrogen and CO 2 . Formate is particularly common in anaerobic habitats, produced as a fermentation product of some species and used as a growth substrate for others. It is crucial compound in many syntrophic associations, in which organisms live close to the thermodynamic limit (for example, sulfate-reducing bacteria and methanogens) |CITS: [18708519][20844539]|. Its redox potential is low (around -420 mV), which allows it to donate an electron for the reduction of fumarate. In eukaryotes formate is produced from a variety of nutrients, and can be fed into a number of biosynthetic pathways. A common source of formate is the catabolism of serine or glycine (via tetrahydrofolate). Another important source is formaldehyde, which is formed by many demethylation enzymes and as a degradation product of methanol. Formate is also produced during sterol synthesis, polyamine synthesis, and tryptophan degradation, and is used during purine synthesis, thymidylate synthesis, and as the source of carbon for methylation reactions via folate and methionine (formate can be assimilated into folate by |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.3| and its carbon transferred to methionine by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13|. Methionine is then converted to |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|, the most common methyl group donor) 31402327.

Synonyms: coenzyme II // triphosphopyridine nucleotide // nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate // NADP-oxidized // NADP-ox // TPN // TPN+ // TPN-ox // nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide-P // NADP(+) // NADP // beta-NADP +
Comment: |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as |FRAME: Cofactors cofactors|. They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes". The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form. |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|).

Interestingly, there is evidence that the creation of large amounts of these compounds may impose a metabolic cost that can negatively impact plant growth |CITS: [11504029][16411958]|, suggesting that plants must finely tune PG biosynthesis to maximize overall fitness. |FRAME: CPD-1142 Salicin| may deter herbivore attack when it is hydrolyzed by beta-glucosidases to |FRAME: CPD-173| in insect guts, possibly leading to the formation of gut lesions 12921436. Compound.name: 5-methyltetrahydropteroyl tri-L-glutamate
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of several cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551.

Comment: 1-(beta-D ribofuranosyl)nicotinamide (often referred to as nicotinamide riboside) is one of three forms of vitamin B 3 : |FRAME: NIACINE|, |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE|, and |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_RIBOSE "nicotinamide riboside"| [more accurately named 1-(beta-D ribofuranosyl)nicotinamide]. These three forms are interchangeable, and are usually used for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: NAD| |CITS: [Elvehjem38][15137942]|. |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_RIBOSE| can be hydrolyzed to form |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| by |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.3| |FRAME: RXN-8441| and |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| can be hydrolyzed to |FRAME: NIACINE| by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.19| (which is not present in humans) |FRAME: NICOTINAMID-RXN| Eukaryotes and prokaryotes produce NAD de novo from |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, respectively, by pathways that bypasses vitamin B3 compounds and instead proceed via |FRAME: NICOTINATE_NUCLEOTIDE| (see |FRAME: NADSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|). Vitamin B3 compounds are used in NAD salvage pathways such as |FRAME: PWY-5381| and |FRAME: PWY3O-4106| |CITS: [13563526][13563527][15137942]|. In populations with a tryptophan-poor diet the NAD de novo biosynthesis pathway is not sufficient to produce the required NAD, making the salvage pathways that rely on vitamin B 3 compounds the main source of NAD.
